AI scientist comparison

Three AI judges (Claude Fable 5.1, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra) read pairs of papers released by five AI scientist systems and picked the more creative paper in each pair. The comparison uses 86 papers sampled from the 410 eligible papers these systems released.

A scientist’s score is its average win rate against the other 4 scientists. Each opponent counts equally, even where fewer pairs were possible.

Small released pools: Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3) has 2 eligible papers; Sakana AI Scientist (v2) has 3 eligible papers. Their scores rest on these few papers, each reused in many pairs.

How much the scores could change with other pairs

These ranges show how much each score could move if different pairs had been drawn. Overlapping ranges mean the order between those scientists is uncertain.

We grew this comparison after seeing earlier results: first from 6 to 10 pairs per matchup, then from 4 to 5 scientists. Earlier votes were kept unchanged. The range formula assumes a sample size fixed in advance, so treat these ranges as rough guides, not 95% confidence intervals.

Statistical method

The calculation treats each judge’s answer to every possible paper pair as fixed and varies only which pairs were drawn. The ranges use Serfling’s bound for sampling without replacement, widened so all 10 matchups are covered at once. Source: Bardenet and Maillard, Concentration inequalities for sampling without replacement, Proposition 2.2 (Serfling’s bound) and the second inequality of Theorem 2.4.

Strengths and weaknesses in the judges’ reasons

Each point sums up what the judges’ saved reasons say about one scientist’s papers. For each scientist, an AI model read the parts of all 572 reasons that discuss that scientist’s papers and grouped the points that recur. A point needed support from at least 8 judgments, covering at least 3 paper pairs and at least 2 judges. A separate AI review then checked 6 randomly chosen cited judgments for each of the 38 points found (a partial match counts as half). One point scored 67% and was dropped. In the other 37, all shown here, 83% to 100% of the checked judgments made the point. The wording was edited after that check. Counts are the judgments cited for each point. One reason can support both a strength and a weakness, because judges weigh tradeoffs. Quotes are copied from the saved reasons. “Preferred in” counts every judgment, so it differs slightly from the ranking, which weights each opponent equally.

Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3)

Preferred in 208 of 216 judgments.

Judges see its two papers as carefully controlled studies that test where their own result comes from instead of only reporting a win. Most parts are familiar and the evidence is narrow; all 8 of its losses came against ScientistTwo.

Strengths: Clear methods with controlled tests; Tests the obvious answer; One or two pieces with no specific precedent; Candid about its limits.

Weaknesses: Narrow evidence; Mostly familiar building blocks; Key move is a standard technique; Adapter paper claims more than it shows.

Evidence and quotes for Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3)

Strengths

  • Useful Clear methods with controlled tests

    Both papers spell out how the method works and support the claimed benefit with controlled comparisons, such as switching the learned part off on the same random seeds.

    Cited in 208 judgments on 36 paper pairs: 66 from Claude Fable 5.1, 70 from Gemini 4 Argon, 72 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “making the learned increment experimentally separable rather than merely asserted”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Surprising Tests the obvious answer

    Instead of only reporting gains, the papers ask where the gains come from: the evolution-strategy paper shows that more than half of its margin comes from the classical method it builds on, and the adapter-merging paper shows the obvious fixes failing before moving the fix to the merging step.

    Cited in 206 judgments on 36 paper pairs: 69 from Claude Fable 5.1, 71 from Gemini 4 Argon, 66 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “the central move is to show the scaffolding supplies 55.8% of the margin and the learned part reverses sign on final return”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • New One or two pieces with no specific precedent

    Judges place most parts in known work but find one or two pieces they can tie only to a broad research area, not to a specific earlier paper. GPT-6 Astra sometimes calls this novelty modest.

    Cited in 132 judgments on 35 paper pairs: 50 from Claude Fable 5.1, 63 from Gemini 4 Argon, 19 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “I can place this particular controller only in mirrored evolution-strategy literature, not confidently in a specific prior paper”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Useful Candid about its limits

    Claude Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon credit the papers for stating their own weak points openly, such as relying on a single training run.

    Cited in 109 judgments on 34 paper pairs: 56 from Claude Fable 5.1, 52 from Gemini 4 Argon, 1 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “transparently documents and isolates these limitations while delivering a complete, falsifiable, and highly effective mechanism”

    Gemini 4 Argon

Weaknesses

  • Useful Narrow evidence

    Each paper tests its claim in one main setting: one test environment and one training run for the evolution-strategy paper, and one synthetic benchmark and one model for the adapter-merging paper.

    Cited in 181 judgments on 36 paper pairs: 54 from Claude Fable 5.1, 56 from Gemini 4 Argon, 71 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “the evidence is confined to one synthetic multi-needle benchmark, a real scope caveat”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • New Mostly familiar building blocks

    Judges find most components in named earlier work, so the credit for New rests on one or two narrow pieces.

    Cited in 143 judgments on 36 paper pairs: 36 from Claude Fable 5.1, 57 from Gemini 4 Argon, 50 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “should not receive novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Surprising Key move is a standard technique

    Some judges, mostly GPT-6 Astra, call the key move standard: switching learning off is the usual test for this question, and picking the context that matches the query is close to ordinary retrieval.

    Cited in 40 judgments on 25 paper pairs: 5 from Claude Fable 5.1, 1 from Gemini 4 Argon, 34 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “the obvious approach is a component ablation; disabling learning is therefore not inherently surprising”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Useful Adapter paper claims more than it shows

    For the adapter-merging paper only, judges, mostly GPT-6 Astra, say a few failed alternatives cannot prove that combining adapters without seeing the query is doomed; some add that choosing context at query time conflicts with the paper’s aim of folding context into the weights once.

    Cited in 38 judgments on 16 paper pairs: 10 from Claude Fable 5.1, 4 from Gemini 4 Argon, 24 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “creating a tension with the stated goal of folding context into weights once before seeing the query”

    Gemini 4 Argon

ScientistTwo

Preferred in 177 of 236 judgments.

Judges see ScientistTwo’s papers as fully written-out methods whose central idea often departs from the obvious fix. The main criticism, pressed hardest by GPT-6 Astra, is that the theory and claims go beyond what the papers show. It won most judgments against each of the three lower-ranked scientists but lost 52 of 60 against Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3).

Strengths: Methods written out and tested; A central idea away from the obvious fix; One piece with no specific precedent; Open about what did not work.

Weaknesses: Theory and claims go beyond the evidence; Signature parts add little in its own tests; Expected path against the strongest rival.

Evidence and quotes for ScientistTwo

Strengths

  • Useful Methods written out and tested

    Judges credit methods given as equations and algorithms and tested against baselines and ablations (tests that remove one part at a time), though some papers leave a key part untested on its own.

    Cited in 202 judgments on 39 paper pairs: 60 from Claude Fable 5.1, 68 from Gemini 4 Argon, 74 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “specifies an actionable update: smooth estimated success rates, retain verified successes, and apply a weighted positive-score update when current rollouts all fail”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Surprising A central idea away from the obvious fix

    Judges often find that the core idea departs from the expected approach for the task, sometimes backed by a result that runs against intuition.

    Cited in 170 judgments on 35 paper pairs: 50 from Claude Fable 5.1, 63 from Gemini 4 Argon, 57 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “attacks a structural claim about phase lock in self-supervised masking and shows a counterintuitive failure of peak-only masking”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • New One piece with no specific precedent

    Across nearly all its papers, judges often find that the most unusual piece can be tied only to a broad research area, not to a named earlier paper.

    Cited in 110 judgments on 38 paper pairs: 39 from Claude Fable 5.1, 50 from Gemini 4 Argon, 21 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “cannot be placed in a specific prior paper, only within the broader subfield genre of learning-augmented online paging”

    Gemini 4 Argon

  • Useful Open about what did not work

    Claude Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon praise papers that openly report components that did not help and variants that failed.

    Cited in 33 judgments on 18 paper pairs: 17 from Claude Fable 5.1, 16 from Gemini 4 Argon.

    “candidly reports that its gate is statistically inert on a frozen base”

    Claude Fable 5.1

Weaknesses

  • Useful Theory and claims go beyond the evidence

    Judges, GPT-6 Astra above all, find guarantees that do not hold as written and mathematical framing that promises more than the experiments show.

    Cited in 131 judgments on 40 paper pairs: 30 from Claude Fable 5.1, 22 from Gemini 4 Argon, 79 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “three central mechanisms suffer from severe internal contradictions where the claimed payoffs do not follow from its own math and tables”

    Gemini 4 Argon

  • Useful Signature parts add little in its own tests

    In about half of its papers (15 of 29), the paper’s own ablations show the distinctive component adding little or nothing over a simpler alternative, such as a constant gate.

    Cited in 96 judgments on 23 paper pairs: 28 from Claude Fable 5.1, 33 from Gemini 4 Argon, 35 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “signature Dual Spectral Risk Gate collapses to a near-constant schedule”

    Gemini 4 Argon

  • Surprising Expected path against the strongest rival

    Mostly in its losses to Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3), judges say the paper takes the expected route of adding known techniques to a baseline.

    Cited in 44 judgments on 15 paper pairs: 19 from Claude Fable 5.1, 15 from Gemini 4 Argon, 10 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “follows the expected multi-heuristic combination template of its subfield”

    Gemini 4 Argon

ScientistOne

Preferred in 124 of 240 judgments.

Judges credit ScientistOne for concrete, implementable methods with some departures from the expected approach, but often find claims that outrun its own numbers, in wins and losses alike. It won 118 of 120 judgments against the two older Sakana systems but none of 60 against Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3) and 6 of 60 against ScientistTwo, where its papers read as small steps along the expected path.

Strengths: Implementable methods with ablations; A departure from the expected solution; One piece with no specific precedent; Unexpected results from its own tests.

Weaknesses: Claims that outrun its own numbers; Familiar building blocks; Own tests undercut the featured part; Small steps along the expected direction.

Evidence and quotes for ScientistOne

Strengths

  • Useful Implementable methods with ablations

    Judges credit methods specified down to equations, pseudocode and parameters, with benchmark results and ablations (tests that remove one part at a time).

    Cited in 138 judgments on 32 paper pairs: 37 from Claude Fable 5.1, 43 from Gemini 4 Argon, 58 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “provides a substantially more actionable algorithm, including the replication rule, sorting key, and scatter construction, together with reported evaluation and alternative-heuristic results”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Surprising A departure from the expected solution

    When it wins, mostly against the older Sakana papers, judges often find that the core idea moves away from the expected solution; in its losses the same moves tend to read as expected.

    Cited in 115 judgments on 26 paper pairs: 30 from Claude Fable 5.1, 44 from Gemini 4 Argon, 41 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “departs centrally from a static global column order by treating column ordering dynamically per row subset via a state-aware prefix trie”

    Gemini 4 Argon

  • New One piece with no specific precedent

    Mostly in its wins (47 of 53), judges find one piece they can tie only to a broad research area; against stronger rivals the same pieces are often traced to known work.

    Cited in 53 judgments on 25 paper pairs: 11 from Claude Fable 5.1, 30 from Gemini 4 Argon, 12 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “I can place only within the emerging LLM-SQL/ADRS reordering literature rather than a specific prior formulation”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • Surprising Unexpected results from its own tests

    Claude Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon credit experimental results that go against expectations, though several of the effects are small.

    Cited in 36 judgments on 13 paper pairs: 14 from Claude Fable 5.1, 22 from Gemini 4 Argon.

    “completely omitting dynamic per-row column reordering in favor of a purely static global column order outperforms dynamic recursive partitioning”

    Gemini 4 Argon

Weaknesses

  • Useful Claims that outrun its own numbers

    Judges often find text that disagrees with the paper’s own tables, or promised features the method does not deliver.

    Cited in 181 judgments on 40 paper pairs: 58 from Claude Fable 5.1, 51 from Gemini 4 Argon, 72 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “the abstract advertises a 'hybrid neuro-symbolic solver that combines LLMs with MCTS' though the described method contains no LLM and the hybrid is only future work”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • New Familiar building blocks

    Judges break most methods into standard parts from earlier work; GPT-6 Astra adds that combining them does not count as new.

    Cited in 168 judgments on 40 paper pairs: 59 from Claude Fable 5.1, 69 from Gemini 4 Argon, 40 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “assembly of familiar components is not itself evidence of new building blocks”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Useful Own tests undercut the featured part

    In 12 of its 17 papers, the paper’s own tests show the featured addition barely helping or a simpler variant doing better, or they never test the addition on its own.

    Cited in 97 judgments on 25 paper pairs: 44 from Claude Fable 5.1, 29 from Gemini 4 Argon, 24 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “its core adjustment improves error only from 0.2463 to 0.2445, while augmentation accounts for a substantially larger difference”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Surprising Small steps along the expected direction

    Almost entirely in its losses to Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3) and ScientistTwo, judges say the paper takes the obvious route for its task and develops it a little further.

    Cited in 80 judgments on 21 paper pairs: 29 from Claude Fable 5.1, 30 from Gemini 4 Argon, 21 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “Hessian scaling and alternating updates develop the expected sensitivity-aware direction rather than substantially redirect it”

    GPT-6 Astra

Sakana AI Scientist (v2)

Preferred in 56 of 214 judgments.

Judges see its three papers as finished but conventional studies. With concrete setups and openly reported negative results, its papers won 54 of 60 judgments against Sakana AI Scientist (v1) but only 2 of 154 against the other three scientists, mainly because results are described in words rather than numbers, the experiments do not test the stated claims, and the findings were predictable.

Strengths: Concrete, runnable setup; An unusual central choice; A negative result as the main finding; Admits its method failed.

Weaknesses: Few numbers, missing details; Experiments do not test the claim; Standard building blocks; Predictable findings.

Evidence and quotes for Sakana AI Scientist (v2)

Strengths

  • Useful Concrete, runnable setup

    Judges, mostly GPT-6 Astra, credit clearly specified experiments, with the training objective, metrics and settings stated, so the proposal can be checked, although some key details are missing.

    Cited in 103 judgments on 36 paper pairs: 17 from Claude Fable 5.1, 18 from Gemini 4 Argon, 68 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “mechanism is concrete and executed: symmetric vs asymmetric noise injection at 10–50% on CIFAR-10/MNIST/Fashion-MNIST with ResNet-18”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • Surprising An unusual central choice

    GPT-6 Astra, much more than the other judges, credits an unconventional choice in two of the papers, such as using smoothness over time to stand in for compositional structure, while noting that the choice is not tied to the task.

    Cited in 46 judgments on 24 paper pairs: 2 from Claude Fable 5.1, 10 from Gemini 4 Argon, 34 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “substituting temporal smoothness is a genuinely unexpected central mapping, independently of whether it works”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Surprising A negative result as the main finding

    Making the failure of the obvious fix the central result reads as a departure from the usual success story, although judges differ on how large a departure it is.

    Cited in 44 judgments on 15 paper pairs: 19 from Claude Fable 5.1, 17 from Gemini 4 Argon, 8 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “by explicitly framing its contribution around negative and inconclusive findings that show where standard hyperparameter tuning and domain transfer fail under environmental variability”

    Gemini 4 Argon

  • Useful Admits its method failed

    For the compositional-regularization paper only, judges credit the paper for stating plainly that its method did not help. GPT-6 Astra also credits it for admitting that its measure may not capture what it claims, but adds that admitting this does not resolve the problem.

    Cited in 21 judgments on 10 paper pairs: 5 from Claude Fable 5.1, 7 from Gemini 4 Argon, 9 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “acknowledges possible misalignment of its measure on page 4, which is valuable, but does not resolve it”

    GPT-6 Astra

Weaknesses

  • Useful Few numbers, missing details

    Results are often described only through figure captions, with almost no numbers; some citations are left as “(?)”, and key settings or promised analyses are missing.

    Cited in 170 judgments on 34 paper pairs: 55 from Claude Fable 5.1, 66 from Gemini 4 Argon, 49 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “the text provides no quantitative tables or numerical values to support its claims”

    Gemini 4 Argon

  • Useful Experiments do not test the claim

    The main experiment often measures something other than what the claim needs; for example, models trained on unrelated image datasets say nothing about pest detection in the field.

    Cited in 168 judgments on 36 paper pairs: 50 from Claude Fable 5.1, 51 from Gemini 4 Argon, 67 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “training ResNet-18 separately on EuroSAT, MedMNIST and CIFAR-10 and then reporting their own accuracies and ERS says nothing about transfer to pest detection”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • New Standard building blocks

    Judges trace most parts to standard practice, such as a robustness score that matches the usual measure of robustness to image distortions, and give little credit for New.

    Cited in 164 judgments on 36 paper pairs: 58 from Claude Fable 5.1, 68 from Gemini 4 Argon, 38 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “are standard practice and the relative-robustness metric from the corruption-robustness literature (ImageNet-C style evaluation)”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • Surprising Predictable findings

    Judges say the conclusions were expected, such as label noise hurting calibration; for the label-noise paper the route itself is also the obvious one.

    Cited in 134 judgments on 31 paper pairs: 44 from Claude Fable 5.1, 48 from Gemini 4 Argon, 42 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “reports the wholly expected conclusion that label noise degrades calibration and asymmetric noise is more harmful”

    Gemini 4 Argon

Sakana AI Scientist (v1)

Preferred in 7 of 238 judgments.

Judges see most of its papers as routine studies on small, familiar setups, such as a parameter sweep or a standard add-on to a toy model. Most claim benefits they never measure, and many are partly unfinished. Its 7 wins came from two papers that report concrete measurements.

Strengths: An occasional unusual direction; Concrete measurements, when present.

Weaknesses: Benefits claimed but not shown; Familiar building blocks; Takes the obvious route; Unfinished manuscripts.

Evidence and quotes for Sakana AI Scientist (v1)

Strengths

  • Surprising An occasional unusual direction

    GPT-6 Astra, more than the other judges, credits a less expected route in a few papers, such as pausing training updates to study grokking (sudden late generalization), but judges say it is never worked out; none of these 15 judgments was a win.

    Cited in 15 judgments on 6 paper pairs: 3 from Claude Fable 5.1, 2 from Gemini 4 Argon, 10 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “replacing updates with extended evaluation is a genuinely unexpected central hypothesis”

    GPT-6 Astra

  • Useful Concrete measurements, when present

    GPT-6 Astra, more than the other judges, credits the few papers that report measured numbers such as timings, losses or memory use. The numbers often support less than the paper claims.

    Cited in 13 judgments on 5 paper pairs: 2 from Claude Fable 5.1, 2 from Gemini 4 Argon, 9 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “mechanism is worked out and quantified: four tasks, three seeds, explicit definitions, Tables 1–3 giving simplification/grokking step timings”

    Claude Fable 5.1

Weaknesses

  • Useful Benefits claimed but not shown

    Abstracts announce improvements that the paper never measures, or that its own tables contradict.

    Cited in 227 judgments on 40 paper pairs: 73 from Claude Fable 5.1, 77 from Gemini 4 Argon, 77 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “empirical results directly refute its abstract and introduction claims of improved training and inference efficiency”

    Gemini 4 Argon

  • New Familiar building blocks

    Judges find the building blocks in standard work, such as the usual grokking and small-language-model training setups.

    Cited in 196 judgments on 40 paper pairs: 64 from Claude Fable 5.1, 78 from Gemini 4 Argon, 54 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “are all standard material from Power et al. and basic deep-learning practice”

    Claude Fable 5.1

  • Surprising Takes the obvious route

    Most papers do what a researcher would try first: a sweep over learning rate, batch size or model size, or a standard loss or module added to a toy model.

    Cited in 190 judgments on 39 paper pairs: 61 from Claude Fable 5.1, 69 from Gemini 4 Argon, 60 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “follows this expected direction directly without any conceptual or empirical departure”

    Gemini 4 Argon

  • Useful Unfinished manuscripts

    Many papers contain unfilled template text such as “RESULTS HERE”, empty sections, truncated sentences or broken figure references.

    Cited in 146 judgments on 35 paper pairs: 61 from Claude Fable 5.1, 67 from Gemini 4 Argon, 18 from GPT-6 Astra.

    “the manuscript's Related Work, Results, and Conclusions sections are empty while the method text is truncated mid-sentence”

    Claude Fable 5.1

How the comparison works

For every two scientists, we drew up to 10 pairs of their papers at random, or all pairs when fewer than 10 exist. Each judge read every pair twice, once in each order, and picked the more creative paper. That gives 6 votes per pair (4 for the 2 pairs Claude Fable 5.1 refused). For each scientist, a pair’s score is the share of votes its paper won. A matchup averages its pairs, and a scientist’s score averages its 4 matchups.

Sampling plan: random seed 2026; 10 pairs per matchup, or all 6 possible pairs for Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3) vs. Sakana AI Scientist (v2); 96 pairs in all.

The judges used version 1 of the New, Useful, Surprising (NUS) rubric. CREST now defaults to version 2, which was not used here.

New, Useful, and Surprising

These concepts are considered jointly in one overall creativity judgment. They are not scored separately; the judge explains the relevant tradeoffs.

New
How hard it is to place the paper’s least familiar building block (a claim, mechanism or mapping) in earlier work. Combining familiar blocks counts toward Surprising, not New. The judge checks this from memory, which can miss prior work.
Useful
Whether the paper explains how its approach works and provides evidence for its claimed benefit.
Surprising
How far the paper’s central idea departs from the obvious way to tackle its question.

Conceptual foundations: Runco and Jaeger (2012), The Standard Definition of Creativity, discusses originality and effectiveness. Acar, Burnett, and Cabra (2017), Ingredients of Creativity: Originality and More, examines surprise alongside originality and value. These works motivate the three ideas; they do not test CREST’s rubric. More detail: the current NUS rubric (v2, not used here) and why we ask for one overall judgment.

Full method: Paper comparison method.

What this comparison leaves uncertain

  • These scientists differ in topics, release dates, underlying AI models and which papers their teams chose to release. Score gaps can reflect any of these differences.
  • Judges read text extracted from each PDF. They did not see figure images, extraction can drop equations or tables, and nobody checked the experiments.
  • The sampling ranges cover only which pairs were drawn. They do not cover judge error, rerun noise, model updates, or whether the rubric captures creativity.
  • The results describe these released papers only. Future papers from the same systems could rank differently.

Cost is estimated from recorded usage at published rates.

Claude Fable 5.1 refused, on safety grounds, to judge 2 paper pairs. Those 2 pairs are scored on the other two judges’ 4 votes, and nothing is filled in for the missing votes. Every request for the 4 refused judgments was billed: $4.13, included in the total.

The total also includes $13.87 for 60 discarded requests from earlier runs. They add no votes.

Judges: Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1, effort high), Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon, thinking level high) and GPT-6 Astra (gpt-6-astra, reasoning effort high). See judge models.

Preferred: How Much of a Learned Evolution Strategy Is the Algorithm It Was Anchored To?

A's central move is to build a learned evolution strategy so that the classical algorithm is exactly recoverable (zero-initialized bounded multiplicative gates, A pages 1, 4) and then to report the decomposition rather than the headline: the identity-gate anchor already supplies 55.8% of the above-reference margin, the learned increment shrinks with budget and reverses sign on final return (A pages 6-8, Table 1 page 9). The obvious approach for A's task would be to report the 1.191 win and the 2.42x budget saving; A instead uses its own construction to undercut that reading, which is a genuine departure in direction and is central rather than incidental. Its least placeable blocks—the success-rate-gated antithetic mirroring and the pair-consistent path normalization mu_path_eff (A page 5, Eq. 3)—I can place only within the mirrored-sampling/CSA subfield rather than a specific formulation, whereas zero-init residual gating and learned recombination weights are placeable in ReZero-style initialization and Lange et al.'s learned ES. A's usefulness is bounded by one environment, one meta-training run, and acknowledged confounds (A page 10), but the attribution mechanism is fully worked out and the negative result is supported by paired seeds. B's task is to speed up CST-based incremental BPE, and the obvious approach—flatten small trees into cache-aligned arrays and replace branchy search with a SIMD compare/movemask/tzcnt kernel—is exactly what B does (B pages 2, 5-6); every block is placeable: Euler-tour DFS interval membership is textbook, flat layouts for small sets are Khuong & Morin (cited, B page 3), the branchless mask pipeline is the simdjson genre, and the fast-path bypass is standard automaton engineering. The only hard-to-place element is the empirical ≤8-node topology statistic (B page 8, Table 2), which is a measurement rather than a mechanism. B is useful in that it is exact across 72 configurations (B page 7), but the payoff over the real baseline is modest (1.123x geomean) and B's own ablation (B page 9, Table 3) shows the named SIMD contribution adds only ~1.009x, with flattening doing the work; figures for the K=8 speedup (1.079x, 1.123x, 1.197x) also differ across sections. Trading A's narrower empirical scope against B's broader but predictable and small engineering gain, A's unexpected, well-instrumented attribution result makes it the stronger creative contribution.

A's task is to speed up incremental BPE; the obvious route is to replace pointer-chasing tree search with cache-friendly flat arrays and branchless SIMD, which is exactly what VD-STrans does (A pages 2, 5–6), drawing directly on Khuong & Morin and simdjson-style bitmask tricks that A itself cites (A page 3) plus standard DFS-interval subtree tests. Its least placeable block is the empirical observation that >99% of Suffix-Successor Trees have ≤8 nodes (A page 8, Table 2), which is a useful but narrow systems finding. The implementation is thorough (code listing A page 14–15, fidelity checks A page 7), yet the payoff is modest and partly undercut by its own evidence: Table 3 (A page 9) shows flattening alone gives 1.128× while the headline SIMD kernel adds only 1.009×, and Fig. 3a reports 1.079× at K=8 versus the 1.123× abstract claim, so the central vectorization mechanism is nearly inert and the numbers are not fully consistent. B's task is learned-ES transfer, where the obvious approach is to report a headline win over CMA-ES; B instead builds an exact identity-gate null control into the architecture via zero-initialized bounded multiplicative residuals (B pages 1, 3–4) and uses it to show that 55.8% of the margin is scaffolding, that the learned increment shrinks with budget (86.5%→44.2%, B page 7) and reverses sign on final return (B page 7, Table 1 page 9), and that meta-learning worked in-distribution but failed to transfer (B page 8). Its components (learned ES à la Lange et al., mirrored sampling, zero-init residuals) are individually placeable, but the pair-consistent path normalization for mirrored draws (B page 5, Eq. 3) and the attribution-by-construction framing are harder to pin to a specific prior work. B's evidence is narrow (one environment, one meta-training run, acknowledged selection bias, B page 10), but it supports exactly the claim it makes and includes clean secondary findings (path normalization is a correctness requirement, stall re-expansion is a null). Overall B departs further from the expected direction with a central move that reframes how such results should be reported, and its demonstrated payoff matches its stated task more faithfully than A's small, predictable, and internally weakened speedup.

Manuscript A demonstrates stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript B when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly relative to each paper's field and task. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task—meta-learning an evolution strategy on cheap low-dimensional analytic functions and transferring it to a high-dimensional continuous-control task—is to parameterize a neural update rule on top of a classical optimizer, benchmark it against a standard external CMA-ES baseline, and claim successful meta-transfer when it wins (A pages 1–2). A departs fundamentally from this expected direction: rather than presenting its 1.191 normalized score (winning 8/8 seeds over the pinned CMA-ES reference) as a triumphant headline, A designs its architecture as an exact subtractive control to deconstruct and refute that headline reading (A pages 1–2, 4, 6–8). By showing that switching the learned gates off on the identical code path still scores 1.107 (accounting for 55.8% of the margin), that the learned contribution decays from 86.5% at generation 1,000 to 44.2% at generation 2,000, and that the learned residual actually degrades final return by 220.7 points despite cutting in-distribution analytic log regret by 50.8% (A pages 6–9), A turns a standard meta-optimization study into a sharp diagnostic localization of transfer failure. By contrast, for B's task—accelerating pointer-based Centroid Search Tree (CST) incremental Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) on modern CPUs—once profiling shows that over 99% of Suffix-Successor Trees contain at most 8 nodes (B pages 2, 8), the obvious systems-engineering approach is to flatten those small pointer trees into cache-aligned contiguous arrays, evaluate the 8 interval checks in parallel with 256-bit AVX2 SIMD instructions, and add a bitmask fast-path for single-byte root transitions (B pages 2–3, 5–6). B executes this standard hardware-optimization playbook directly. For New, B's core mathematical and algorithmic building blocks—Prefix Consistency, Suffix-Successor Trees, the Prefix Last-Token Condition, the Monotonic Path Property, DFS entry/exit interval linearization [L_t, R_t), and CST fallback—are directly placeable in a single named prior work, Jiang & Gong (2026) (B pages 2–5). B's remaining blocks—flattening small search trees into contiguous SIMD vectors, branchless AVX2 range comparison via _mm256_cmpgt_epi32, _mm256_movemask_ps, and tzcnt, replacing slow hardware vpgatherdd instructions with unrolled scalar loads, and root bitmask bypassing—are standard formulations placeable in the SIMD parsing and data-structure literature (such as Khuong & Morin, 2015 and Langdale & Lemire, 2019, cited on B page 3; B pages 5–6, 15). In A, while separable CMA-ES (Hansen, 2016) and Deep-Sets permutation-equivariant encoders (Lee et al., 2018) are established building blocks (A pages 2, 4), its least placeable building blocks—specifically, the pair-consistent evolution-path normalization (A page 5, Equation 3) compensating for neutral variance bias under success-rate-gated partial mirrored sampling, and the zero-initialized bounded multiplicative residual gate formulation g(v) = exp(ln 2 * tanh(3v)) applied across separable CMA-ES recombination weights, step-size/mean updates, and diagonal covariance exponents to guarantee exact code-path subtractability (A pages 4–5)—are harder to place specifically, as they cannot be named in a single prior paper beyond the broader subfield literatures of evolution-strategy adaptation and meta-learned optimizers. For Useful, both papers present complete implementations and ablations, with a clear tradeoff between B's broader benchmark coverage and A's stronger mechanism-to-payoff alignment. B evaluates 12 tokenizers across 3 datasets to show a 1.123x geometric-mean speedup over the CST baseline with 100% fidelity (B pages 7–8, Table 1). However, B's component ablation (B page 9, Table 3) reveals that its central proposed mechanism—the branchless AVX2 SIMD interval kernel—contributes only a marginal 1.009x (0.9%) speedup over simply flattening the pointer tree into a scalar array (Flat-Scalar at 1.128x vs. Flat-SIMD at 1.138x), with the rest of the gain coming from pointer elimination and the simple root bitmask (+5.1%). As B's C++ code listing shows (B page 15, lines 756–766), because candidate history offsets are non-contiguous, the kernel must spill the SIMD index vector to stack memory, execute an 8-iteration scalar gather loop, and reload into AVX2 registers, largely neutralizing the vector comparison advantage. A has a narrower empirical scope—testing transfer on a single 704-dimensional Brax Ant task with one meta-training run per configuration (A page 10)—but its mechanisms are fully worked out and rigorously support every claimed payoff, including demonstrating that pair-consistent path normalization prevents a catastrophic 0.294 score drop and step-size freeze at generation 500 (A pages 8–9, Table 1) and cleanly isolating meta-learning's early-budget head start from its asymptotic transfer deficit.

For B's task—meta-evolving a neural evolution strategy on cheap low-dimensional analytic functions and transferring it zero-shot to a 704-dimensional Brax Ant control policy—the obvious approach is to show that the meta-learned optimizer beats a classical CMA-ES baseline (scoring 1.191 vs. 1.000 across 8/8 seeds) and claim successful out-of-distribution scale transfer (B pages 1, 6). B departs sharply at the center of its thesis: it constructs the optimizer so that all learned outputs can be switched off exactly at the source level, using this null control to dismantle its own headline win. It reveals that 55.8% of the margin over reference CMA-ES comes from the classical separable CMA-ES anchor and fixed sampling scaffolding alone (1.107 vs. 1.000), and exposes a striking metric and horizon inversion where the learned modulation provides an early-budget head start (86.5% of the excess at generation 1,000) that decays with budget and reverses sign on final solution quality, finishing 220.7 return lower than the unmodulated anchor after generation 1,216 (B pages 1, 6–8). For New, A's core algorithmic building blocks—Prefix Consistency, Suffix-Successor Trees, the Monotonic Path Property, Depth-First Search (DFS) entry/exit interval checks, and CST fallback—are explicitly taken from Berglund & van der Merwe (2023) and Jiang & Gong (2026) (A pages 2–5), while its 8-lane AVX2 branchless interval check (`_mm256_cmpgt_epi32`, `_mm256_movemask_ps`, `tzcnt`) and unrolled scalar gather (avoiding slow `vpgatherdd` microcode) are standard techniques in the SIMD search literature such as Khuong & Morin (2015) (A pages 3, 5–6, 14–15). A's least placeable block is the specific empirical mapping of LLM vocabulary Suffix-Successor Trees (observing that >99.1% have <= 8 nodes) into 256-bit Flat Decision Vectors with an Aho–Corasick root bitmask bypass (A pages 5–6, 8). In B, while separable CMA-ES, Deep Sets equivariant encoders, and mirrored sampling are established in their respective literatures (B pages 2–4), B's least placeable blocks are harder to place to standard templates: specifically, its pair-consistent evolution-path variance normalization `mu_eff^path = (sum_{pairs}(w_a - w_b)^2 + sum_{unpaired} w_i^2)^{-1}` coupled with success-gated partial antithetic mirroring to prevent cumulative step-size adaptation (`p_sigma`) neutral-variance deflation under arbitrary recombination weights (B page 5 Eq. 3; page 8), alongside its zero-initialized bounded multiplicative residual gate formulation `g(v) = exp(ln 2 * tanh(3v))` designed for exact scaffolding subtraction across a 70x dimension jump (B page 4 Eq. 2). For Useful, both manuscripts present fully worked-out mechanisms with solid empirical verification, though with different tradeoffs. A provides complete C++ AVX2 and ARM Neon implementations and evaluates 72 configurations across 12 tokenizers and 3 text domains, achieving a 1.123x geomean speedup over the CST incremental baseline (`Inc-orig`) and up to 23.64x over heap BPE with 100% fidelity (A pages 7–10, 14–16). However, A's component-wise ablation (Table 3, A page 9) reveals a notable tradeoff: simply flattening the tree into a pointerless scalar array (`Flat-Scalar`) achieves a 1.128x speedup, whereas adding the central AVX2 SIMD vectorization (`Flat-SIMD`) reaches 1.138x—meaning SIMD vectorization itself contributes only a marginal 1.009x (0.9%) gain, while pointer elimination and the 1-byte atomic root bypass (reaching 1.197x on the ablation subset) do the heavy lifting. Conversely, every mechanism in B is essential to its claimed analytical and algorithmic payoff: B's seven controlled configurations prove that omitting pair-consistent path normalization causes catastrophic step-size collapse (dropping the score from 1.191 to 0.897 and freezing return after generation 500), that diagonal covariance adaptation remains vital even when severely under-sampled at N=256 in D=704 (+0.360 paired score), and that meta-learning genuinely succeeded in-distribution (-50.8% log regret on training functions, -28.4% on held-out functions) before failing to generalize its horizon tradeoffs during high-dimensional transfer (B pages 7–10).

B has a narrow overall edge because its structural observation leads to a concrete, supported computational improvement, rather than merely an unusual assembly of familiar techniques. A combines separable CMA-ES, identity-centered residual gates, permutation-equivariant conditioning, mirrored sampling, and a same-code null control (A pages 4–5). Its least-placeable individual design choice is the success-rate-dependent mirroring policy; I can locate that only in adaptive/mirrored evolution-strategy literature, not a particular prior formulation. B combines incremental last-token selection, DFS interval tests, flat arrays, SIMD masks, an atomic bypass, and a tree-search fallback (B pages 4–6). Flat, branchless searching is specifically recognizable from Khuong and Morin’s Array Layouts for Comparison-Based Searching. B’s least-placeable substantive claim is instead the measured concentration of suffix-successor trees below eight nodes: I cannot identify an earlier specific result beyond the subfield of BPE vocabulary-structure profiling. Neither manuscript deserves novelty credit simply for combining its ingredients. For A’s stated attribution task, the obvious approach is to disable learning while preserving the surrounding optimizer. Its exactly recoverable anchor implements that approach particularly cleanly. The genuinely unexpected finding is that learning improves anytime performance but worsens mean final quality (A pages 6–7). For B’s exact incremental-tokenization task, the obvious approach is to optimize the existing search traversal and memory layout. Its departure is to exploit the vocabulary topology to avoid traversal altogether on almost all vocabulary entries, testing ordered candidates simultaneously while retaining search for the tail. This remains recognizable systems engineering, but the structural observation centrally determines the alternative execution strategy. Both mechanisms have meaningful evidence. A’s identity gates isolate a reported +0.083 paired anytime increment, positive on all eight evaluation seeds, while the anchor finishes 220.7 return higher on average. That answers its local attribution question well. However, configuration selection on those seeds, one meta-training run, and separately retrained secondary ablations restrict stronger causal and transfer conclusions (A page 10). B supplies interval-selection details, an implementation, reported exact token-sequence agreement, and a 1.123× improvement over the relevant incremental baseline—not just the much larger heap-baseline comparison (B pages 5–7 and 15). Its component study usefully shows that flattening supplies most of the improvement: SIMD increases the ablation-subset speedup only from 1.128× to 1.138× (B page 9). Consequently, I credit topology-aware representation and execution, not a novel SIMD primitive. Claims of single-cycle execution or demonstrated ARM performance exceed the supplied evidence; the cutoff experiment is not an ARM benchmark (B pages 9 and 16). A offers the sharper diagnostic reversal, but B more convincingly turns its least-familiar structural finding into an actionable mechanism with demonstrated payoff. That supports the narrow overall choice.

B: How Much of a Learned Evolution Strategy Is the Algorithm It Was Anchored To? · Sakana Agentic Scientist (v3)

Preferred: How Much of a Learned Evolution Strategy Is the Algorithm It Was Anchored To?

A builds on incremental BPE, DFS interval validation, flat SIMD search, atomic fast paths, and a centroid-tree fallback (A pages 4–6). The layout and branchless-search ingredients are recognizable in cache-aware search work such as Khuong and Morin’s Array Layouts for Comparison-Based Searching. Its least placeable block is the empirical finding that almost all relevant suffix trees fit within eight candidates (A page 8); I cannot locate that particular result more narrowly than empirical BPE algorithm engineering. B builds on separable CMA-ES, population-equivariant and coordinate-shared networks, identity-centered multiplicative residuals, and mirrored sampling (B pages 4–5). These are familiar optimizer and residual-learning ingredients. Its least placeable claim is the particular budget- and metric-dependent decomposition of transferred performance into scaffolding and learning (B pages 6–8), which I can place only in learned-optimizer evaluation literature, not a specific earlier result. Neither manuscript earns novelty merely from assembling familiar components. A offers a worked, actionable optimization: flatten candidate trees, gather historical timestamps, test intervals in parallel, and select the deepest valid candidate while retaining the original fallback. Reported reference-token agreement and a 1.123× geometric-mean improvement over incremental BPE support a practical throughput payoff (A page 7). Its component ablation is especially informative: flattening produces 1.128×, whereas adding SIMD raises that to 1.138× on the ablation subset (A page 9). Thus the contribution is substantially a data-layout improvement, not the much larger algorithmic advance suggested by comparisons with heap BPE. ARM performance and broader serving savings are not demonstrated by the supplied experiments. B’s useful mechanism is experimental identification rather than simply a better optimizer: forcing every residual gate to one removes learned influence while preserving the nonlearned implementation. This supports a meaningful comparison between the full strategy’s 1.191 score and the identity anchor’s 1.107, with a positive paired learning increment on all eight evaluation seeds (B pages 4–6). The mean terminal-return reversal—3488.5 versus 3709.2—then shows that the learning increment buys earlier progress rather than uniformly better optimization (B pages 7–9). This conclusion remains narrow: one transfer environment, one meta-training run, configuration selection on the evaluation seeds, and missing paired terminal-return statistics limit generalization; several secondary ablations also confound mechanism changes with retraining (B page 10). For A’s task, the obvious approach is cache-conscious and vectorized acceleration of incremental searches; replacing search with exhaustive parallel validation of unexpectedly tiny candidate sets is a useful but fairly direct departure. For B’s attribution task, the obvious approach is an unlearned baseline or module ablation, so the identity control alone is not especially surprising. The more consequential departure is the supported finding that successful in-distribution learning and improved transferred anytime performance coexist with inferior final solutions and a large nonlearned contribution. A supplies a credible engineering payoff and a distinctive structural observation, but B’s exact intervention turns a performance claim into a qualitatively different, operationally useful conclusion about when learning helps. That substantive diagnostic contribution, rather than its critical presentation, makes B the stronger overall creative work.

A's central move is to build a learned evolution strategy whose learned part can be switched off exactly (zero-initialized bounded multiplicative residuals on separable CMA-ES, A pages 1, 4) and then to report the decomposition rather than the headline: the identity-gate anchor already scores 1.107 of the 1.191, the learned increment shrinks with budget and reverses on final return (A pages 6-7, Table 1 page 9). The obvious approach for its task is to report a learned-optimizer transfer win; A instead uses an exact null control to show most of the margin is scaffolding, a departure central to the paper, and it is unusually honest about confounds (single meta-training run, selection bias, page 10). The least placeable blocks (pair-consistent path normalization for mirrored draws, Eq. 3 page 5; the exact-identity attribution control) are placeable only at the level of the mirrored-sampling/learned-ES literature rather than a specific formulation. B assembles well-known components—Lanczos top-eigenvector extraction, gradient-difference curvature proxies, EMA server drift momentum (B pages 3-4)—into a federated SAM variant; the direction is a modest, predictable engineering combination. More importantly, B's usefulness is undercut by its own tables: KSCV is worse than no drift control at every participation rate (Table 9, B page 13) and removing it improves accuracy (Table 5, page 9); pure gradient-SAM (Wmax=0) is within ~1 pt of the default and the applied perturbation mostly tracks the gradient (page 7, Table 8 page 13); FedWMSAM beats the full method in the 200-round ablation (Table 5); and Table 1 margins of 0.1-0.4 pts carry no variance (page 5). The abstract's 'immunity to staleness' and 'matches or outperforms' claims therefore do not follow from the evidence, leaving B in need of repair, whereas A's mechanism, control, and payoff are worked out and internally consistent even though the payoff is a negative/attributional result. A is the stronger creative contribution overall.

The least specifically placeable methodological blocks are A’s success-conditioned mirroring rule and B’s mapping of phase disagreement to intervention demand. I can place these only broadly in adaptive evolution-strategy and synchronization-based control literature, respectively, not identify an exact prior source for either. Neither manuscript’s unusual assembly alone establishes New, and B’s canonical-form terminology does not make its underlying rotation mathematics new. For A’s stated attribution task, the obvious approach is a matched learned-versus-disabled ablation; for B’s efficient reasoning-stabilization task, it is a structured recurrent controller or a cheaper continuous-time solver. A makes the expected control exact by construction, but its central unexpected direction is the discovery that learning buys earlier progress while worsening the eventual solution. B’s interpretation of phase mismatch and persistent spectral energy as reasoning risk and trustworthy evidence is a more adventurous conceptual departure than merely replacing dense exponentials with analytic rotations. The tradeoff nevertheless favors A because its central scientific payoff follows much more securely from the mechanism and experiments. Setting every multiplicative gate to one removes learning without changing the surrounding implementation. The resulting comparison separates the reported score of 1.191 into an anchor score of 1.107 and a paired learned increment of approximately 0.083, positive on all eight evaluation seeds; the anchor nevertheless finishes 220.7 return higher (A pages 6–9). This supports a concrete, consequential distinction between successful anytime acceleration and successful final-quality transfer. One environment, reused configuration-selection seeds, and a single meta-training run limit generalization; separately retrained ablations also confound several secondary mechanism claims, although not the inert-gate control (A page 10). B does demonstrate a useful implementable controller: its block exponential is exact, reported GSM8K accuracy improves from 41.62% to 50.87%, and latency measurements support inexpensive execution (B pages 5, 7, 10 and 16). However, those results do not establish several load-bearing explanations. The claim that independent rotation-decay blocks impose no expressivity restriction fails for defective generators and context-dependent families lacking a common eigenbasis (B page 5). The contraction proof concerns an unforced flow under shared conditioning, not stability of the driven autoregressive system or preservation of answer correctness (B page 15). Moreover, the spectral gate becomes nearly constant on the frozen backbone, with no demonstrated advantage over constant gating; the co-adaptation experiment does not establish the claimed universal do-no-harm property (B pages 8–9). Thus B’s distinctive spectral-to-semantic mapping remains substantially less supported than its practical accuracy improvement. A offers less architectural departure, but turns familiar machinery into a supported and unexpected revision of what its optimizer’s apparent transfer success actually means, giving it stronger overall creative quality.

Its building blocks are hypernetwork-generated LoRA adapters, interference under composition, MaxSim addressing, and relevance- and boundary-aware localization (A pages 3–4). The adapter and retrieval mechanisms are recognizable from HINT and ColBERT; its least-placeable claim is the specific diagnosis that composition governs this binding failure, which I can locate only broadly in neural binding/interference literature, not a particular prior result. B combines a Merton mixture, median/mode inversion, stratified inverse-CDF sampling, variance matching, and mean-reset numerical restarts (B pages 4–5). Most are standard statistical or numerical constructions. Its hardest-to-place block is the horizon-independent weak-error claim for mean-reset trajectories; I can place that only broadly in numerical SDE analysis, not an established theorem. Thus neither manuscript earns New credit merely for assembling familiar components, and B’s unusual theoretical proposal remains distinct from whether it is correct. For A’s task, obvious approaches include improving adapter capacity or binding supervision, or retrieving relevant text for the prompt; for B’s tractable-mixture forecasting task, obvious approaches include loss-appropriate mixture statistics and variance-reduced sampling. A’s central departure is to put retrieval inside weight composition, changing when the system decides which information to express rather than enlarging its information generator. Query-based routing is familiar, so this is not a wholly unexpected invention, but it is a substantive redirection. B largely develops the expected analytical direction; its less-expected mean-reset restart is ancillary to its three headline contributions. A also supplies a relatively direct mechanism test: query-conditioned selection alone raises reported exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, with relevance placement and delimiter alignment bringing it to 0.98 (A page 6). These interventions explain how the improvement arises rather than merely asserting a payoff. However, family-best comparisons, training collapses, and one synthetic task cannot establish that query-blind composition necessarily destroys bindings or that no better head or loss could succeed (A pages 4, 7–8). The supported result is a strong local routing benefit, not a structural impossibility theorem. B provides valuable fixed-checkpoint ablations and across-seed estimator comparisons, supporting practical gains from replacing Monte Carlo selection and improving candidate coverage (B pages 6–7). Its one-step median inversion is sound in principle. Nevertheless, repeatedly using each candidate’s same quantile across time does not establish faithful joint Merton-path sampling, so oracle coverage gains have a narrower meaning than distributional fidelity (B page 4). More seriously, resetting stochastic states to their means removes variance; it cannot generally preserve convergence to the original process for nonlinear observables, invalidating the claimed general weak-error argument (B pages 5 and 11). The variance penalty also helps at 28 days but worsens the reported 14-day results (B page 12), limiting the stability claim. B’s operational improvements remain useful, but its theoretical guarantees need repair. Overall, A’s more unexpected relocation of the decision mechanism, coupled with its clearly demonstrated local payoff, outweighs its limited scope and overextended bottleneck interpretation.

Thus neither manuscript deserves novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components, and the specificity of identifiable precedents does not establish a decisive novelty advantage by itself. For A’s inference-improvement task, the obvious approach is to exploit the available mixture distribution with loss-matched estimators and variance-reduced sampling. While spherical Langevin dynamics and CLIP-x0 guidance are standard formulations in named works (e.g., Girolami & Calderhead, 2011; Bansal et al., 2023), A's least placeable building blocks—probing directional score curvature specifically along the CFG difference vector d_c at t=T and repelling batchwise spatial Query Gram matrices at pure noise—cannot be placed in a single prior paper, sitting instead in the broader subfield literature of training-free diffusion seed optimization and cross-attention layout control (adjacent to SAIL, Jeon et al., 2024; DivIn, Li et al., 2026; and InitNO, Guo et al., 2024; A page 2–3). Manuscript B breaks down into: (1) chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-concatenation merging (B page 1, 3); (2) negative-control hypernetwork read-out/head modifications and auxiliary binding/margin losses (B page 3–4); (3) query-conditioned token-level late-interaction (MaxSim) scoring over frozen encoder token representations to select which chunk's adapter dominates the merge (B page 2, 4); and (4) relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunk cutting (B page 4, 6). B's core routing block is directly placeable in specific named works—ColBERT and ColBERTv2 (Khattab et al., 2021; Santhanam et al., 2022b; B page 2, 4)—while its chunk-boundary and windowing heuristics belong to standard retrieval chunking and the hypernetwork adapter subfield (e.g., HINT, Ivison et al., 2023; B page 2). Thus, A relies on less specifically placeable mathematical building blocks than B. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of mitigating CFG mode collapse without retraining is either intervening along the reverse denoising trajectory t in [T-1, 0] via step-wise particle guidance or running unconstrained Euclidean optimization on pixel-level Tweedie L2 differences at t=T (A page 1–3); for B's task of fixing multi-needle retrieval in context-to-LoRA hypernetworks, the obvious approach is increasing the capacity of the hypernetwork's read-out/output head or adding training-time auxiliary binding losses to separate co-resident facts (B page 1–4). B makes a sharp, central conceptual departure by using those two intuitive directions as falsifiable negative controls—showing both hit a 0.52 exact-match superposition ceiling—and reframing long-context weight internalization as a merge-time routing problem solved without retraining via late-interaction addressing (B page 2, 5–7). A departs from standard trajectory interventions and scalar pixel-space potentials by operating strictly at t=T on the sqrt(D)-hypersphere using directional CFG curvature and compact 64x64 cross-attention Query Grams, uncovering the unexpected mechanistic result that raw t=T Query Grams yield higher full-system diversity than full-resolution Tweedie x0 Grams because Tweedie clean estimates at pure noise are noise-dominated and low-rank (A page 5, 15). I can connect that claim only to the adapter-interference literature, not name an earlier demonstration. B builds from directional finite differences, spatial-Gram repulsion, fidelity penalties, and manifold Langevin updates (B pages 4–5). Manifold Langevin is specifically established in Girolami and Calderhead’s work; B’s least-placeable block is probing velocity sensitivity along the normalized conditional-minus-unconditional guidance direction. I can place that only broadly in score-geometry/Jacobian-regularization research, not an exact prior formulation. Neither receives novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach would be improving key–value binding through adapter capacity, supervision, or interference-aware merging. Its central departure is postponing selection until the query arrives and routing generated weights rather than retrieving prompt text. Query-based selection is familiar in retrieval, so this is a meaningful relocation rather than an entirely unexpected principle. For B’s task, the obvious approach would be reducing or annealing guidance, repelling denoising trajectories, or optimizing initial seeds. B extends the last direction by coupling batch layout repulsion to norm-constrained initialization; this is a substantive extension, but initialization-time intervention itself is already established. A provides a relatively direct connection between its intervention and success: query-conditioned selection raises exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, while relevance placement and boundary alignment reach 0.98 (A page 6). These component comparisons support routing as an effective fix for the stated retrieval task. Important qualifications remain: implementation details and replicated uncertainty are missing, configurations are evaluated once, and training collapse occurs (A pages 4–5, 7). Moreover, the decoder still receives the query, so failed capacity and loss variants cannot establish that query-blind composition is fundamentally incapable of retrieval. A demonstrates a practical bottleneck under its budget, not a universal impossibility. B supplies more explicit update equations and meaningful evidence across architectures, including diversity gains and experiments identifying norm restoration as a stabilizer (B pages 7, 9–10). However, its distinctive explanatory claims are less secure. Its own ablations show that ordinary post-hoc rescaling performs similarly to tangent dynamics, while the proposed fidelity hinge is dormant by default and ineffective when activated; the replacement CLIP objective only partially recovers lost quality (B pages 9, 16). The directional Jacobian norm derived on B page 14 is not a Rayleigh quotient and does not distinguish contraction from expansion, weakening the claimed basin-escape explanation. Fidelity is also a genuine tradeoff rather than uniformly preserved, as the DiT precision and feature-distance results show (B page 18). Finally, the approximately 3% overhead claim on B page 10 is unreconciled with the 63.7% default overhead reported on B page 15. Overall, A’s narrower but more directly supported reframing outweighs B’s inventive geometric formulation and broader demonstrations. The choice rests on the alignment between A’s central conceptual move and its supported local payoff, not on benchmark scale or the raw magnitude of incomparable metrics.

A assembles three fixes to the spectral-sphere optimizer SSO (A pages 1-5): tangent projection of momentum, a closed-form stable-rank gradient added as an isotropization force, and a 2D Krylov reduction of the Lagrange root-finding. Each block is placeable: tangent-projected momentum is standard Riemannian momentum (Bécigneul & Ganea, Kong et al. style), stable-rank regularization appears in SRN (Sanyal et al. 2019) and MSign, and the dual root-finding is SSO's own formulation; the 2×2 Krylov collapse is the least placeable piece but is a straightforward subspace trick. The direction is exactly what a competent follow-up to SSO would take (speed up the bisection, add rank regularization), so Surprising is low. On Useful, the evidence is large in scale but internally shaky: the headline rank-preservation claim is undercut by Table 2 where SSO retains higher stable rank (144.0) than RMTS (89.4) (A page 7); the momentum-transport ablation in Table 6 shows Riemannian transport losing to plain Euclidean accumulation and tangential projection (A page 16); the 2D solver leaves a constraint residual of 0.394 so the tangent constraint is essentially not enforced and is patched by retraction (A page 5, page 16); ablation losses (5.79, 4.17) are on scales incompatible with the main results (A pages 8-9); and the exact 2.0× / 14,400 s timings with identical losses look suspiciously clean. The mechanism is partly worked out but the claimed payoff does not cleanly follow. A offers the stronger creative reframing, although B provides a more explicit implementation and more extensive transfer evidence. A decomposes into hypernetwork-generated LoRAs, MaxSim retrieval, query-dependent routing, relevance-driven span placement, and aligned chunking (A pages 3–4). B decomposes into Fisher scatter weighting, trace-target covariance shrinkage, relative-Mahalanobis and energy scores, robust standardization, and gated weighted addition (B pages 4–5). These are largely recognizable primitives: MaxSim appears specifically in ColBERT, while B’s covariance rule is standard identity-target linear shrinkage. A’s least specifically placeable block is relevance-peak “atom” placement, which I can locate only in retrieval-guided span-selection literature, not a particular prior work; its underdescription limits confidence that it constitutes a distinct algorithm. B’s least specifically placeable block is the mid-layer residual correction, whose role belongs to OOD score-fusion literature and whose mathematical gate is a standard negative hinge. Neither paper earns novelty simply from assembling these components. For A’s task, the obvious approaches are improving adapter binding/capacity or retrieving query-relevant chunks; its departure is to use retrieval to select generated weights at composition time rather than supply retrieved text or retrain the generator. For B’s task, the obvious approach is regularized feature-distance detection combined with classifier confidence. Its class-aware weighting and relocation of gating from features to scores develop that expected direction. A’s unexpected central move is therefore the placement and diagnostic role of routing—not the invention of query-dependent retrieval. A supports this move with a targeted intervention: frozen-encoder token similarities select the relevant chunk adapter without new trainable parameters, raising reported exact match from 0.52 to 0.91; relevance placement and boundary alignment then reach 0.98 (A pages 4 and 6). The unsuccessful head and loss alternatives provide useful evidence for a local composition bottleneck. Nevertheless, one evaluation per configuration, training collapses, and the synthetic single-fact task constrain that conclusion (A pages 4–5 and 7–8). These experiments do not establish the stronger assertion that query-blind composition necessarily destroys binding: the downstream model still receives the query, and unsuccessful finite-budget alternatives cannot prove impossibility. B’s mechanism is more fully actionable: its equations specify stable distance estimation and complementary score fusion. Reported CIFAR-100 FPR95 falls from 4.17% to 2.17%, while fixed-setting improvements across adaptation strategies and backbones support transfer beyond one feature geometry (B pages 6–8). However, not every advertised mechanism receives equally strong support: deployed tied shrinkage essentially matches tied empirical covariance, at 4.38% versus 4.37% FPR95 (B page 7). Its DS derivation establishes additivity for the specified zero-ignorance sigmoid masses, not a general inability of DS methods to incorporate reliability weighting (B page 11). These qualifications temper the explanatory claims without negating the detector’s demonstrated utility. Overall, B supplies useful engineering of established scoring ingredients, but A’s controlled relocation of retrieval into weight composition yields a more distinctive, empirically grounded explanation of its task’s failure mode. That explanatory departure narrowly outweighs B’s stronger specification and broader demonstrated applicability.

Its central departure is to postpone selection until the query arrives and use token-level retrieval to choose weights rather than prompt text. Query-dependent retrieval itself is familiar, so the surprise lies in relocating the decision and challenging the presumed upstream bottleneck. For B’s task, the obvious approach is Fisher regularization or structured, matrix-free solves plus variance reduction. Replacing empirical curvature estimation with analytically orthonormal features is a more adventurous central shortcut; its PCG and control-variate components follow expected directions. A supports its intervention with a clear mechanism and useful component comparisons: frozen-encoder MaxSim selects the relevant chunk’s adapter, relevance-based placement focuses its content, and aligned boundaries prevent fragmented facts. This is substantial evidence for the particular intervention, although not for a universal impossibility of query-blind storage: a merged model could in principle retain bindings and use the downstream query. B reports meaningful benchmark improvements and informative variance-reduction ablations (B pages 8–9), but its principal generalization needs mathematical repair. B assumes that premise for its classical families (B pages 5 and 14), yet ordinary Gamma statistics include log x, and Beta statistics include log x and log(1−x); finite Laguerre or Jacobi polynomial vectors cannot be an invertible linear transformation of those statistics. Thus the claimed exact non-Gaussian natural-parameter update does not follow. The dense mapping also costs O(m²), with the stronger complexity claim requiring additional structure acknowledged on page 5. Reported payoff is conditional rather than uniformly stabilizing: adding control variates worsens Poisson KL from 2.846 to 2545.219 at N=50 (B page 15). Its least placeable block is the particular frequency-times-squared-string-length priority, which I can place only broadly in heuristic trie/data-layout optimization, not identify as an established formula (B pages 4–5). Neither receives novelty credit merely for assembling familiar components. While every general component in A has roots in dense retrieval or PEFT, A's least placeable block—relevance-peak atom placement for hypernetwork-emitted weight updates—can only be placed at the level of the broader subfields of span-based dense retrieval (e.g., Ma et al., 2022) and hypernetwork parameter generation rather than a specific prior formulation. Manuscript B relies on: (1) VoxelNet and image backbones projected into a Bird's Eye View (BEV) grid with a CenterPoint detection head (B page 4, page 6, page 7), which is standard material in multi-modal 3D detection (Zhou & Tuzel, 2017; Yin et al., 2020); (2) MLP-based 2D Cartesian coordinate positional encodings (B page 5), which is standard material across BEV vision transformers; (3) Euclidean distance transforms and binary masks over rasterized HD map channels (B page 5), which is standard material in map-aware autonomous driving perception; and (4) a sigmoid-gated convex combination of two feature embeddings added to a BEV feature map (B page 5, page 6). Even B's least placeable block—gated additive fusion of rasterized HD map embeddings and Cartesian coordinate embeddings in BEV—is a standard formulation appearing across numerous works in multimodal BEV perception and gated multimodal units. Regarding Surprising, for Manuscript A's task of resolving multi-fact retrieval failures in long-context hypernetwork-generated LoRA adapters, the obvious approach is to increase the hypernetwork's read-out/output-head capacity to represent multiple key–value bindings or add auxiliary training losses that supervise multi-target separation (A page 2, page 3). For Manuscript B's task of leveraging HD semantic maps to improve 3D bounding box geometry in BEV object detection, the obvious approach is to encode rasterized HD map channels alongside spatial coordinates and fuse them into the BEV feature map prior to the detection head (B page 2, page 5). Manuscript A makes a sharp, central departure from its obvious direction: it demonstrates that modifying the generator architecture and training objective both fail because query-blind adapter merging inherently induces weight-space superposition of co-resident facts, and it instead reframes weight-space context internalization as an inference-time routing problem solved by repurposing ColBERT-style token-level MaxSim inside the hypernetwork's frozen encoder to select which chunk's adapter dominates the merge (A page 2, page 4, page 7). By contrast, Manuscript B follows the expected direction for map-aware BEV fusion almost directly, and its only unexpected twist—that raw binary map masks marginally outperform Euclidean distance transforms by +0.0002 (B page 1, page 9)—is an incidental preprocessing ablation detail rather than a central conceptual departure. Regarding Useful, Manuscript A's central proposal is a parameter-free, training-free query-conditioned merge-time router using late-interaction MaxSim over the frozen encoder's token states, paired with relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunk boundaries (A page 4). The mechanism is fully worked out and validated through a falsifiable experimental design across 30 valid trained models under a fixed 3-hour single-GPU budget across context lengths from 128 to 65,536 tokens (A page 4, page 6, page 8). Its claimed payoff follows decisively: while read-out/head redesigns plateau at 0.32 exact-match accuracy, auxiliary training losses plateau at 0.46, and the strongest query-blind merge reaches a ceiling of 0.52, adding query-conditioned MaxSim selection alone lifts accuracy to 0.91, and adding atom placement and delimiter-aligned cuts reaches 0.98 (A page 6 Table 1, page 7 Figure 3), with training-collapse variance transparently separated from the accuracy ceiling (A page 7, page 8 Figure 4). Manuscript B's central proposal is Hybrid Semantic-Cartesian Positional Encodings (HSC-PE), which passes BEV Cartesian coordinates and HD map Euclidean distance fields through MLPs and fuses them via a learned sigmoid gate before a CenterPoint head (B page 5, page 6, page 7 Algorithm 1). While B's pipeline is coherent enough to run and clear a competition threshold (0.1763 aggregate score, B page 8 Table 1), its claimed payoffs suffer from internal contradictions and missing evidence. Even accounting for the tradeoff that A is evaluated on a synthetic benchmark whereas B tackles a multi-sensor real-world driving dataset, A's surprising cross-domain routing assembly and rigorously demonstrated diagnostic payoff make it far more creative overall.

Single-configuration evaluations, training collapses, and the synthetic single-fact-query setting limit the causal and generalization claims (A pages 4 and 7–8); query-time routing also changes the originally query-independent composition regime. B reports useful evidence for textual boundary alignment: 0.8356 Kendall tau and a decline to 0.7920 when succeeding-code context is removed (B page 8). However, its proposed global mechanism needs substantive repair. Page 6 allows multiple markdown cells per gap while invoking ordinary linear sum assignment, whereas page 8 asserts strict one-to-one matching. Moreover, the continuous expectations and row-wise argmax described on page 6 do not themselves enforce global assignment constraints, and ordering multiple markdown cells within one gap remains unresolved. Consequently, the reported performance can support useful local alignment without validating the advertised global-resolution explanation. A’s bounded but intelligible intervention therefore offers the stronger overall creative contribution: an unexpected central reframing with directly relevant empirical support, rather than a familiar structural formulation whose claimed mechanism conflicts with its implementation description.

Both manuscripts build largely from recognizable components. Its least specifically placeable ingredient is the two-sided code-gap representation: I can place it in notebook-ordering and document-insertion research, but cannot name an exact predecessor. B uses hypernetwork-generated adapters, MaxSim addressing, relevance-guided span placement, and delimiter-aligned chunking (B pages 3–4). HINT and ColBERT provide identifiable precedents for adapter generation and late interaction; B’s least specifically placeable ingredient is relevance-profile “atom” placement, which I can locate only broadly in retrieval-guided span selection. Neither manuscript deserves originality credit simply for assembling familiar ingredients unusually. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to score markdown against code context and predict insertion positions or pairwise order; its boundary-anchor formulation is a useful but relatively natural refinement. For B’s task, the obvious approach is to improve the hypernetwork’s capacity or binding supervision while preserving query-blind adapter composition. B’s central departure is to move selection to composition time, using retrieval scores to control which weights are expressed rather than which text enters the prompt. Query-dependent retrieval itself is familiar, but this relocation constitutes a substantive redirection of the proposed solution. A provides evidence that two-sided context helps: removing the succeeding code cell reduces reported Kendall tau from 0.8356 to 0.7920 (A page 8). However, its claimed global-consistency mechanism needs repair. Ordinary linear sum assignment imposes one-to-one matching, whereas the task permits several markdown cells in the same gap. A page 6 acknowledges that multiplicity but supplies neither an appropriate capacity formulation nor a within-gap ordering rule; it also describes expectation and argmax decoding as enforcing global bipartite constraints, although neither does so. These are substantive inconsistencies, not extraction artifacts. Consequently, the reported benchmark performance supports boundary-based alignment more convincingly than the manuscript’s central explanation of why global matching works. Independent local encoding also avoids whole-notebook concatenation without demonstrating recovery of distant contextual dependencies. B’s mechanism is more coherent and more directly connected to its reported payoff: frozen query–chunk MaxSim scores suppress irrelevant adapters at merge time. Moreover, unsuccessful head and loss variants establish only a budget-limited empirical bottleneck—not an impossibility theorem for query-blind composition. Nevertheless, B’s central redirection has a substantially better-supported working mechanism.
