A's central move is to locate the multi-needle failure of context-to-LoRA hypernetworks in the query-blind adapter merge and fix it with a parameter-free MaxSim router at composition time (A pages 1-4); the building blocks—ColBERT late interaction, LoRA merging/LoraHub, HINT-style hypernetworks—are each placeable, but using late interaction as a merge-time router over hypernetwork-generated adapters is not something I can place more narrowly than the adapter-composition subfield, and the paper's own related-work framing (A page 3) treats it as a new use of the primitive. The obvious approach for A's task would be to enlarge the generator head or add binding losses; A runs those as negative controls and shows they plateau at 0.32/0.46 below the 0.52 query-blind ceiling, while selection alone lifts accuracy to 0.91 and 0.98 with chunk-level fixes (A pages 5-7, Table 1, Figure 3), with a coherent superposition explanation and acknowledged limits (synthetic benchmark, one model, collapse mode on A pages 7-8). B's central move—taxonomy-and-prototype-weighted margins My,j = τ·V·(1−T) extending Menon et al. logit adjustment (B pages 4-5)—is readily placeable: taxonomic hierarchies for long-tail (Wu et al. 2020, which B cites), class-similarity-aware margins, and prototype-based confusion priors are standard in the long-tail/fine-grained literature, so its least placeable block is only subfield-level. B's own ablation undercuts its payoff: removing the logit adjustment costs only +0.0018 while removing augmentation costs +0.0242 (B page 7, Table 2), it admits no comparison to a plain frequency-based LA baseline (B page 9), and several Table 1 baselines have no reported numbers. B's honesty is commendable but means the mechanism's demonstrated usefulness is near nil, and the direction (inject a hierarchy prior into logit adjustment) is the expected one for its task. A therefore wins on a harder-to-place central mechanism, a clearly supported payoff with falsifiable controls, and a diagnostic reframing (routing, not capacity) that departs from the obvious architecture/loss route.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and tasks, Manuscript A demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript B when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. Regarding New—judging only individual building blocks rather than their combination—both manuscripts largely draw from established primitives, though A's least placeable block is less standardized than B's. In B, every building block can be traced to a specific named work or standard textbook formulation: logit adjustment via additive margin subtraction comes directly from Menon et al. (2020) (B page 3, page 5); quantifying taxonomic similarity as the normalized count of shared hierarchy levels from kingdom to genus (B page 4, Eq. 1) is a standard tree-similarity formulation in hierarchical classification (e.g., Wu et al., 2020, B page 1); averaging L2-normalized features across layers to form class prototypes and cosine similarity matrices (B page 5, Eq. 2) is standard in prototypical networks and multi-layer feature fusion; and scaling logit margins by pairwise confusion or class difficulty (B page 5, Eq. 3) appears in the dynamic logit adjustment literature (e.g., Zhang et al., 2024b; Low et al., 2025, B page 1, page 3). In A, the core blocks also come from named works: context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-axis adapter concatenation (A page 1, page 3) follow hypernetwork instruction tuning (HINT, Ivison et al., 2023) and adapter merging (Huang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023), while token-level maximum cosine similarity (MaxSim) scoring (A page 2, page 4) comes directly from ColBERT (Khattab et al., 2021; Santhanam et al., 2022b). However, A's supporting block—relevance-profile 'atom' placement, which shifts the internal span representation from which the hypernetwork constructs a chunk's weight adapter onto a token-level relevance peak alongside generator-delimiter-aligned cuts (A page 4, page 6)—cannot be pinned to a single named equation and is placeable only at the broader subfield level of span-based dense retrieval and hypernetwork representation pooling. Regarding Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task (resolving multi-fact retrieval failures in chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetworks) is to increase the hypernetwork's read-out/output head capacity or add auxiliary training losses that supervise key-value binding and penalize distractor interference (A page 2, page 3); the obvious approach to B's task (long-tailed fine-grained species classification without foundation-model leakage) is to modify class-frequency logit adjustment margins using taxonomic tree distances or empirical class confusion priors (B page 1, page 3). B stays close to this expected path, assembling taxonomic distance and offline visual prototype cosine similarity into a multiplicative logit margin $M_{y,j} = \tau \cdot V_{y,j} \cdot (1 - T_{y,j})$ (B page 5, Eq. 3), with only the modest conceptual twist of penalizing visually similar but taxonomically distant species more heavily than within-genus neighbors. In contrast, A makes a sharp, central departure: it first proves that the obvious architectural and training-loss approaches fail because query-blind adapter merging superposes co-resident facts in weight space (A page 2, page 6, page 7), and then repurposes ColBERT-style token-level late interaction from document retrieval as a parameter-free, inference-time router inside a frozen encoder's representation space to select which generated weight adapter dominates composition (A page 3, page 4). Regarding Useful, A's central mechanism is thoroughly validated with a decisive empirical payoff, whereas B's central mechanism yields an almost negligible payoff and suffers from structural gaps. A tests 30 valid trained models across four mechanism families under a strict three-hour single-GPU budget and fixed ~2B base model (A page 4, page 5). Using two falsifiable negative-control families, A shows that head redesigns plateau at 0.32 exact match, auxiliary binding/selection losses plateau at 0.46, and the strongest query-blind merge (incorporating redundancy weighting, competitive gating, and magnitude priors) hits a hard ceiling of 0.52 (A page 3, page 6, Table 1). Introducing query-conditioned MaxSim routing at merge time alone lifts accuracy from 0.52 to 0.91, relevance-profile atom placement raises it to 0.93, and delimiter-aligned chunking reaches 0.98 across context lengths from 128 to 65,536 tokens without adding parameters or retraining (A page 6, page 7, Figure 3). In B, although the equations and offline-online training algorithm are clearly specified (B page 4–6, Eq. 1–4, Algorithm 1) and evaluated on a realistic 1,010-species benchmark (iNaturalist 2019, B page 6), the ablation study reveals that removing the entire proposed logit adjustment degrades Top-1 Error by only 0.0018 (from 0.2445 to 0.2463), whereas standard data augmentation accounts for 0.0242 (B page 7, page 8, Table 2). Furthermore, as B candidly acknowledges (B page 9), it omits a baseline comparison against standard frequency-based logit adjustment (Menon et al., 2020), leaving unproven whether its taxonomic-visual margin beats static frequency scaling. Worse, B's margin $M_{y,j}$ is extracted offline before fine-tuning (B page 5, page 6) and is completely symmetric between classes ($V_{y,j} = V_{j,y}$ and $T_{y,j} = T_{j,y}$) with no class-frequency term, contradicting the central claim that it asymmetrically shifts decision boundaries to prevent common head species from cannibalizing rare tail species (B page 2, Figure 1; page 8, Figure 3). Weighing the tradeoffs, B deserves credit for evaluating on a large-scale real-world ecological dataset, providing explicit mathematical equations, and transparently reporting its near-zero ablation delta and missing baseline (B page 5, page 7–9), whereas A relies on a single synthetic multi-needle benchmark, assumes single-fact queries, and describes its sub-mechanisms (such as atom placement and negative-control heads) in prose without formal equations (A page 4, page 8). Nevertheless, A's creative diagnosis of weight-space superposition, its unexpected cross-domain synthesis of token-level late interaction as a zero-parameter merge-time weight router, and its rigorous, falsifiable empirical payoff (lifting accuracy from 0.52 to 0.98) far outweigh B's incremental and empirically marginal heuristic.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and tasks, Manuscript A demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript B across New, Useful, and Surprising considered jointly. Regarding New (evaluating individual building blocks rather than their combination), Manuscript A relies on: (1) context-to-LoRA hypernetworks that emit per-chunk low-rank adapters and merge them along the rank axis (A pages 1–3), placeable in specific hypernetwork and adapter-composition papers such as HINT (Ivison et al., 2023) and LoRAHub (Huang et al., 2023); (2) token-level late-interaction MaxSim scoring (A pages 2–4), placeable in specific information retrieval works (Khattab et al., 2021; Santhanam et al., 2022b); (3) negative-control read-out heads and multi-target margin losses (A page 4); and (4) relevance-profile atom placement paired with generator-delimiter-aligned chunking to localize the span representation driving a generated weight adapter (A page 4). Its least placeable block—using a token-level relevance peak within a frozen early-exit hypernetwork encoder to position the adapter-generating span ('atom') alongside merge-time routing—can only be placed broadly at the subfield level of hypernetwork context internalization and span-pooled adapter generation rather than in a single specific prior work. By contrast, Manuscript B breaks down into: (1) an LSTM (or simple RNN/attention variant) trained with MSE loss on synthetic arithmetic strings (B pages 2, 5–8), which is standard textbook deep learning material (Goodfellow et al., 2016; Vaswani et al., 2017); and (2) its least placeable block, an auxiliary loss penalizing the mean squared difference between successive hidden states, L_comp = (1/(T-1)) sum ||h_{t+1} - h_t||^2 (B page 2, Eq. 1). Although B labels this 'compositional regularization,' mathematically it is a standard temporal smoothness or activation-stabilization penalty widely found in standard sequence-modeling formulations and RNN regularization literature. Thus, A's least placeable building block is harder to place specifically than B's. Regarding Useful, Manuscript A's central proposal is to resolve multi-needle retrieval failures in chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetworks via a parameter-free, merge-time late-interaction (MaxSim) router in the frozen encoder's representation space, supported by relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunk cuts (A pages 2–4). The mechanism is fully worked out and validated under a strict three-hour single-GPU controlled protocol across 30 valid trained configurations spanning 128 to 65,536 tokens (A pages 3–7). The claimed payoff follows decisively: whereas redesigning the hypernetwork read-out/head plateaus at 0.32 exact-match accuracy, auxiliary binding/selection supervision reaches 0.46, and the strongest query-blind merge hits a superposition ceiling of 0.52, adding query-conditioned MaxSim selection at merge time jumps accuracy to 0.91 alone and 0.98 with the two chunk-level components, without retraining or adding parameters (A pages 5–7, Table 1). A also transparently documents run-to-run collapse variance and benchmark scope limitations (A pages 4, 7–8). In contrast, Manuscript B's central proposal—enforcing compositionality in arithmetic evaluation by penalizing successive hidden-state differences ||h_{t+1} - h_t||^2 (B page 2)—does not work. Conceptually, penalizing state changes across time steps encourages constant/smooth hidden trajectories rather than hierarchical or algebraic composition, directly conflicting with arithmetic operations that require discrete state updates. Empirically, B reports that the regularizer fails to improve upon the ~84% baseline test accuracy, degrades accuracy at higher weights (lambda), and fails on increased operator complexity (B pages 1, 3–4, 6–7). Furthermore, B leaves key experimental evidence incomplete in the text: aside from the ~84% baseline figure, exact accuracy and loss values across ablations are omitted from the prose and left to visual plots not recoverable as numbers in the text, and the numerical tolerance defining 'correct prediction' for MSE regression accuracy is never specified (B page 3). While B offers a tradeoff of honesty in reporting negative results (B page 4), A provides falsifiable negative controls alongside a mechanism that actually solves its task. Regarding Surprising, for Manuscript A's task of fixing multi-needle fact retrieval in context-to-LoRA hypernetworks, the obvious approach would be to increase the hypernetwork's read-out/output head capacity or add supervised binding and contrastive distractor losses during training (A pages 1–3). A departs sharply from this expected direction in two ways: first, it rigorously proves that those obvious architectural and training-loss interventions fail (staying at or below the 0.52 query-blind ceiling because query-blind weight merging structurally superposes co-resident facts; A pages 5–7); second, it repurposes ColBERT-style token-level MaxSim—a primitive from text retrieval—as a parameter-free, inference-time router over hypernetwork-generated weight adapters (A pages 2–4). For Manuscript B's task of improving compositional generalization on arithmetic expressions, the obvious approach would involve hierarchical/tree-structured networks, neuro-symbolic routing, meta-learning, or substructure consistency training (B pages 1–2). B instead applies a simple temporal smoothness penalty to a flat LSTM and reports that it fails (B pages 2–4). While framing a manuscript around a negative result departs from standard positive-result reporting, the technical failure of a state-smoothing penalty on multi-operator arithmetic is predictable rather than a compelling conceptual leap. Weighing these qualities and tradeoffs together, B's candid reporting of a negative result on a simple temporal penalty is far outweighed by A's diagnostic falsification of expected architectural/loss fixes, its unexpected cross-domain assembly of late-interaction retrieval with weight-space adapter merging, and its thoroughly supported empirical payoff.

To evaluate New, we break each manuscript into its constituent building blocks and examine the least placeable block. Manuscript A relies on an LSTM sequence-to-value network trained on synthetic arithmetic expressions (A page 2), a penalty on the mean squared difference between consecutive hidden states $L_{comp} = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|h_{t+1}-h_t\|^2$ (A page 2, Eq. 1), and standard ablations over embedding dimension, attention, RNN vs. LSTM units, and dropout (A pages 5–8). Although A terms $L_{comp}$ "compositional regularization," this exact mathematical building block—penalizing the squared norm of differences between successive recurrent hidden states—already appears in specific recurrent regularization works, notably Temporal Activation Regularization (TAR) in Merity et al. (2017, Regularizing and Optimizing LSTM Language Models) and norm-stabilization regularizers in Krueger and Memisevic (2016). Manuscript B combines chunked context-to-LoRA hypernetwork generation and rank-axis adapter merging (B pages 1–3; placeable in hypernetwork adapter works such as Ivison et al., 2023 HINT, and LoRAHub, Huang et al., 2023), token-level late-interaction MaxSim scoring (B pages 2–4; placeable in ColBERT, Khattab et al., 2021, and ColBERTv2, Santhanam et al., 2022b), controlled negative-control families such as co-resident digit-margin losses (B page 4), and relevance-profile atom placement over delimiter-aligned chunks (B pages 4, 6). B's least placeable building block—shifting the hypernetwork adapter's source representation "atom" onto a token-level relevance peak within a delimiter-aligned chunk so the emitted weight update encodes the queried fact rather than neighboring context (B pages 4, 6)—cannot be traced to a specific prior paper and is placeable only at the broader subfield level of hypernetwork context internalization and token-level retrieval. For Useful, Manuscript A proposes adding $L_{comp}$ to the mean squared error objective to encourage additive compositional representations on unseen arithmetic combinations (A page 2). However, this mechanism is conceptually counterproductive—penalizing $\|h_{t+1}-h_t\|^2$ forces recurrent states to remain static across time steps rather than composing new operators and operands—and the claimed payoff fails to materialize: higher regularization weights $\lambda$ do not improve test accuracy and sometimes degrade learning, while increasing operator complexity breaks both baseline and regularized models (A pages 1, 3–4). Even evaluated as a diagnostic negative report, A leaves its evidence in need of repair because, aside from noting an approximate 84% baseline test accuracy (A page 3), the text provides only qualitative figure descriptions with no exact numerical tables or quantitative metrics for its $\lambda$ sweeps, operator-complexity breakdown, or supplementary ablations (A pages 3–8). By contrast, Manuscript B's central mechanism—using a parameter-free, merge-time MaxSim address inside the hypernetwork's existing frozen encoder representation space to route which chunk's generated LoRA adapter dominates the weight merge, paired with relevance-profile atom placement and delimiter-aligned chunking (B pages 1–4)—is thoroughly worked out and achieves a strongly supported payoff. Across 30 valid models trained under an identical three-hour single-GPU budget spanning 128 to 65,536 tokens (B pages 4–6), B demonstrates that query-blind read-out/head redesigns (0.32 exact match), auxiliary binding/selection losses (0.46), and the strongest query-blind merge (0.52) all stall at a superposition ceiling, whereas parameter-free query-conditioned MaxSim selection alone lifts accuracy from 0.52 to 0.91, atom placement reaches 0.93, and delimiter-aligned cuts reach 0.98 (B pages 5–7, Table 1). For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of improving compositional generalization in neural arithmetic evaluation would be introducing structural/modular architectural inductive biases or compositional data augmentation and reporting a positive accuracy gain. A departs from surface expectations by reporting a negative result that its regularizer and standard capacity/attention tweaks fail (A pages 1, 3–6), but the failure of a smoothness penalty that resists state transitions during sequential arithmetic is mechanically predictable. For B's task of resolving multi-needle binding failures in context-to-LoRA hypernetworks, the obvious approach would be increasing the hypernetwork's head capacity (e.g., slot read-outs or factorized key-value heads) or adding auxiliary training supervision to separate co-resident facts (B pages 2–4). B makes a far more unexpected and central departure: it implements those exact intuitive directions as falsifiable negative-control families to prove that upstream capacity and training losses cannot overcome query-blind weight superposition, and instead repurposes ColBERT-style token-level MaxSim—a text retrieval primitive—as a training-free, merge-time router over generated weight adapters (B pages 2–6, 8–9). Weighing the relevant tradeoffs, while A commendably embraces transparent negative reporting across multiple basic architectural variations (A pages 4–8) and B is confined to a single synthetic multi-needle benchmark and a single ~2B base model subject to occasional training-collapse variance that must be mitigated by restarts and magnitude-prior pinning (B pages 4, 7–8), B's diagnostic rigor, well-supported mechanism, and cross-subfield synthesis make it far stronger overall.

A offers the stronger overall contribution because its central change has a substantially better-supported connection to its task, despite familiar ingredients and an overextended causal interpretation. A’s building blocks are hypernetwork-generated adapters, MaxSim retrieval, query-dependent adapter weighting, and relevance- and boundary-aware span selection (A pages 3–4). Generated adapters and MaxSim are recognizable from HINT and ColBERT; their assembly is not itself evidence of New. A’s least-placeable claim is the experimental localization of retrieval interference to query-blind composition: I can place that only broadly in adapter-interference and neural-binding research, not identify a prior work establishing this particular diagnosis. B combines an LSTM arithmetic regressor with a successive-hidden-state penalty and an interpretation of smoothness as additive compositionality (B page 2). The penalty already appears as temporal activation regularization in Merity et al.’s Regularizing and Optimizing LSTM Language Models. B’s least-placeable block is the smoothness-to-compositionality mapping, which I can locate only broadly in representation-regularization research, rather than a specific established formulation. Thus, B’s unusual interpretation deserves consideration independently of whether it works. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to improve binding through the adapter generator or its training objective; for B’s task, it is to encode arithmetic structure or constrain representations to obey a composition law. A instead postpones selection until the query can determine which adapter enters the weights. This is natural from a retrieval perspective but meaningfully redirects context internalization away from storing every fact in one query-blind composition. B’s replacement of structural constraints with temporal smoothness is also an unconventional central move; neither that departure nor its negative outcome should be dismissed merely because the intended improvement failed. The decisive tradeoff is the demonstrated mechanism. A specifies how token-level similarities route adapters and reports a directly relevant ablation: selection raises exact match from 0.52 to 0.91, with span placement and aligned boundaries reaching 0.98 (A page 6). Its head and loss controls strengthen the practical diagnosis. Nevertheless, single evaluations, training collapses, and the restricted synthetic setting limit confidence and generality (A pages 4–5 and 8). These experiments do not establish that query-blind composition inherently destroys retrievability: the downstream model still receives the query, and unsuccessful alternatives under one budget cannot rule out better binding mechanisms. B provides an implementable objective and useful evidence that this particular penalty does not improve arithmetic generalization (B pages 2–4). However, minimizing successive-state differences encourages smoothness—and permits constant states—not a rule for composing arithmetic components. Lower penalty values therefore do not establish the compositional representations claimed on B pages 3–4. The unspecified accuracy tolerance and incompletely characterized compositional split further restrict the negative conclusion. A’s supported, actionable relocation of selection consequently outweighs its overclaiming; B’s unexpected mapping remains insufficiently grounded to make its failure comparably informative.

The penalty itself is specifically recognizable as temporal activation regularization in Merity et al.’s Regularizing and Optimizing LSTM Language Models; its least-placeable block is the interpretation of temporal smoothness as compositionality, which I can situate only broadly in representation-regularization research, not identify as an established formulation (A page 2). Its least-placeable claim is the task-specific diagnosis that query-blind adapter composition governs multi-needle failure; I can place that broadly in adapter-routing and binding-interference research, but cannot confidently name a prior work establishing this diagnosis. Thus neither manuscript warrants credit for an unprecedented primitive, and B’s unusual assembly belongs to Surprising rather than automatically establishing New. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to encourage structural representations through architecture or a consistency regularizer; A largely follows that direction, with the negative result providing a modest reversal. For B’s task, obvious approaches include improving context encoding and adapter merging, or retrieving relevant text. B’s central departure is to use retrieval to choose which generated adapter enters the weights at query time, rather than enlarging the generator or adding retrieved text to the prompt (B pages 3–4). Query-aware retrieval is familiar, but relocating the selection decision to weight composition is a substantive change in direction. The usefulness distinction is more decisive than primitive novelty. A specifies an implementable penalty and reports that reducing it does not improve accuracy, sometimes worsening performance (A pages 2–3). That is a useful narrow negative finding. However, minimizing successive-state differences encourages nearly constant states, not an operator-sensitive compositional representation; therefore lower penalty values do not establish the compositionality claimed in its interpretation. The reported progression from 0.52 to 0.91 with selection alone, then to 0.98 with supporting components, connects the mechanism to a concrete payoff rather than merely reporting a lower proxy loss (B page 6). Important qualifications remain: single evaluations per configuration, training collapses, and one synthetic benchmark limit reliability and scope (B pages 4–5 and 8). Moreover, failed capacity and loss variants cannot prove a structural impossibility: a query-blind adapter could preserve several bindings for the query-aware decoder to resolve, contrary to B’s strongest language on pages 3 and 7. Nevertheless, B’s bounded empirical contribution survives that overstatement. Its meaningful relocation of retrieval, supported by component-level performance comparisons, provides a more actionable creative advance than A’s weakly grounded compositionality proxy and consequently restricted negative finding.

Its least specifically placeable operative rule is the success-dependent mirroring probability: I can locate this only broadly in adaptive/mirrored evolution-strategy literature, not identify an earlier identical formulation. Its principal training mechanisms map directly to Ho et al.’s DDPM and Goodfellow et al.’s adversarial-training formulation. B’s hardest-to-place claim is instead that very low dimensionality intrinsically amplifies perturbation damage; I cannot identify an established source for that premise. That potentially unusual claim should be distinguished from its familiar interventions, rather than denying it novelty simply because it is unsupported. Neither manuscript earns novelty merely from assembling its ingredients. For A’s stated attribution task, the obvious approach is a learned-off ablation; for B’s robustness task, it is adversarial augmentation followed by perturbation-strength and capacity sweeps. A therefore does not make a radical methodological departure simply by conducting an ablation. Its more unexpected central move is showing that apparent transfer success becomes a budget-dependent head start whose advantage reverses on final solution quality (A pages 6–8). B largely follows the expected intervention sequence, without deriving a mechanism specifically addressing its proposed low-dimensional vulnerability. A makes its attribution mechanism concrete: pinning every multiplicative gate to one removes learned modulation while retaining the same classical core and fixed machinery. The reported anytime scores—1.191 for the full method and 1.107 for the identity control—and the positive paired increment on all eight seeds support a local, implementation-specific learned contribution. The control’s 220.7-higher final return also establishes a practically important distinction between faster progress and a better endpoint (A pages 6–7). These conclusions remain limited by configuration selection on the evaluation seeds, one meta-training run, one transfer environment, and separately retrained auxiliary ablations (A page 10); they do not establish universal transfer failure or isolate every component causally. B supplies a reasonably actionable augmentation recipe, but its evidence does not establish the advertised clean-preserving robustness. Its perturbed evaluation compares generated samples against perturbed reference data, which does not directly measure the output-consistency objective stated earlier (B pages 4 and 6). The baseline lacks perturbed metrics, every reported perturbed KL divergence is infinite, and average clean KL rises from 0.418 to 0.965 in the final configuration (B page 7). Lower perturbed Frechet distance among modified configurations is useful partial evidence, but cannot resolve those gaps. Thus, despite B’s harder-to-source dimensionality premise, A more successfully converts a substantive, somewhat unexpected finding into a controlled and usable scientific conclusion. That connection between mechanism, evidence, and revised interpretation supports the overall choice.

Even A's least placeable building blocks—iteratively connecting unreached terminals to an existing partial tree via multi-source shortest paths and sampling from a restricted top-K candidate list during rollouts—are standard formulations placeable in specific classical works: the Takahashi–Matsuyama (1980) shortest-path heuristic for Steiner trees and the Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure (GRASP; Feo & Resende, 1995) for Steiner tree construction. A makes a more unexpected and central departure: first, it diagnoses that prototype transport in CLIP feature space remains dominated by object categories and actively strips them via a supervised Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) trained against 100 k-means clusters of pristine frozen CLIP embeddings (A page 2, 4–5); second, it repurposes the vision transformer's final-layer negative self-attention entropy as a zero-FLOP perceptual saliency weight for a patch segmentation head trained jointly on synthetic fractional box-overlap targets and real-MOS Multiple Instance Learning (MIL), using the resulting Minkowski-pooled worst-region severity to dynamically sharpen prototype transport temperature (A page 5–6). For New, we examine the least placeable building blocks of each manuscript without judging their combination. B's building blocks—representing states as partial trees, expanding to unreached terminals via multi-source Dijkstra from current tree vertices (B page 4–5), UCT selection (B page 5), and randomized greedy rollouts over the top-K closest terminals (B page 5)—are all directly placeable in standard combinatorial optimization literature, specifically the Takahashi-Matsuyama shortest-path Steiner tree heuristic and Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures (GRASP) combined with MCTS. Regarding Surprising (departure from the obvious approach to each task), for Manuscript A's task of ordering tabular rows and columns to maximize LLM KV-cache prefix overlap, the obvious approach is static cardinality-based column sorting followed by lexicographical row sorting (as in GGR) or black-box evolutionary permutation search (as in AdaEvolve; A page 2). A departs from static column ordering by allowing different row branches in a prefix trie to select different subsequent columns dynamically and bounding search cost via integer vectorization and a 500-row lookahead cutoff (A pages 2, 4–5). While dynamic per-partition column selection is a sensible algorithmic refinement over static global column orderings, it remains an expected greedy/beam-search progression for trie construction. For Manuscript B's task of zero-shot generalist graph anomaly detection (GGAD) under severe Graph Structure Shift (GSS), the obvious approach would be to train deeper multi-hop parametric GNN encoders, apply spectral band-pass filters, or append standard absolute-deviation topological features ($|F|$ or $|z_{FR}|$) weighted more heavily whenever local 1-hop affinity disagrees with higher-order topology (B pages 2–3, 8). A offers the stronger overall creative contribution, although its supported achievement is narrower than its headline claims. Its building blocks are endpoint-relative analogue transfer, FFT decomposition, content/distance weighting, reliability-conditioned residual gates, and validation-selected blending (A pages 5–6). The least readily placeable block is the mapping from neighbour disagreement, boundary mismatch, and retrieval distance to local correction strength: I can place its principle in reliability-conditioned forecast combination and mixture-of-experts gating, but cannot name a specific earlier work containing that mapping. B comprises bounded-width prefix search, completed-subset filtering, and ordered-sequence memoization (B pages 4–6). Even its least routine operation—keeping the cheapest representative of each completed subset—is recognizable as standard best-cost-per-state duplicate pruning in graph search and subset dynamic programming. This comparison concerns the individual mechanisms, not novelty credited merely for assembling familiar tools. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to retrieve similar histories and blend their continuations with the foundation forecast; for B’s task, it is conflict-aware greedy scheduling followed by conventional search over alternative orderings. A makes a meaningful, though not radical, directional departure by treating retrieval as an optional, frequency- and timestep-specific correction rather than a whole-trajectory contribution. B’s subset-based diversity control is central and potentially useful, but remains closer to familiar search-space reduction; avoiding neural inference is not itself an unexpected scheduling strategy. Its ablations also permit scrutiny of the proposed mechanisms. However, monolithic residuals and simpler gates perform nearly as well, limiting the demonstrated necessity of the elaborate decomposition and modulation (A pages 14–15). The safety guarantee applies only to the combined validation objective, not both test metrics: two datasets regress on at least one metric (A pages 6 and 15). Training on benchmark training splits and using target-domain validation calibration also qualify the end-to-end zero-shot claim. These limitations leave a usable forecasting refinement, rather than the claimed universal protection against negative transfer. B’s potential payoff requires more substantial repair. The manuscript does not establish that a completed subset and its scalar makespan constitute a sufficient scheduling state: different orderings can leave different resource or dependency-release times, so the cheaper prefix need not dominate every continuation (B pages 4–5). Moreover, convergence on an unordered subset does not produce cache hits when the cache key is the ordered sequence, undermining the explanation for exponentially increasing memoization efficiency (B pages 5–6). The reported makespan remains potentially encouraging, but the score lacks a defining formula, workload-level comparisons are missing, and the purported filtering ablation changes other search components simultaneously (B pages 6–8). Its 150-second runtime supports, at most, offline batch scheduling, as its limitations acknowledge (B page 9). Thus A’s comparatively traceable mechanism and demonstrated, qualified gains outweigh B’s interesting diversity heuristic whose state-validity and efficiency explanations are not established.

B makes a central, unexpected departure by extracting and repelling spatial composition priors via Query-Query Gram matrices strictly at pure Gaussian noise t=T—where one would not expect cross-attention queries to already encode actionable inter-sample spatial layout structure—and coupling this with directional curvature probing along the guidance vector and hyperspherical norm preservation (B pages 3–5). While A's Riemannian Langevin sampler is standard in manifold MCMC and diffusion literature (e.g., Girolami & Calderhead 2011; De Bortoli et al. 2022) and its CLIP-x0 / attention alignment penalties appear in diffusion guidance works (e.g., Bansal et al. 2023; Chefer et al. 2023), its least placeable blocks—formulating batch-wise repulsion over spatial Query self-similarity Gram matrices strictly at the pure-noise state t=T, alongside probing directional score curvature specifically along the normalized CFG vector d_c at t=T—cannot be placed in a single prior formula and are placeable only at the level of two broader subfield literatures: training-free cross-attention layout control (such as Hertz et al. 2022) and latent initialization sharpness mitigation (such as Jeon et al. 2024). Every building block in B—including its least placeable block, post-hoc grid search for an F1-optimal classification threshold combined with multi-resolution checkpoint ensembling—is common knowledge and standard textbook material across applied machine learning and multi-label classification literature (e.g., Pillai et al. 2013 for F-measure threshold tuning; Dietterich 2000 for ensembling). Regarding Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task (mitigating mode collapse and layout stereotypy in CFG diffusion models) is to apply step-wise guidance, condition annealing, or particle repulsion across intermediate latents along the reverse denoising trajectory t in [T-1, 0], or to perturb initial noise in Euclidean space using pixel-level Tweedie distances (A pages 1–3). For B's task (multi-label artwork classification under hierarchical label relationships and severe false-negative omissions), the obvious approach from the academic ontology literature is to train with an explicit asymmetric or hierarchical box-embedding loss, while from a practical competition standpoint it is to train a classifier head on pre-extracted visual features and tune the decision threshold on a validation set (B pages 1–4). B departs from the academic framing of its own introduction by abandoning explicit hierarchical losses after reporting that seven internal search branches failed, retreating to a standard BCE-trained MLP with scalar threshold tuning (B pages 2, 7–8). A’s operative blocks are a binary-cross-entropy MLP, validation-set threshold search, and multiresolution/checkpoint averaging (A pages 4–6). Even its most specialized operational claim—lowering the threshold to improve F1—has a specifically recognizable antecedent in Lipton et al.’s “Thresholding Classifiers to Maximize F1 Score”; the architecture and averaging are also standard formulations. B likewise uses familiar ingredients: finite-difference sensitivity probes, Gram-based repulsion, hinge penalties, and projected Langevin updates (B pages 4–5). Its least-placeable block is the particular mapping from inter-seed spatial Query-Gram dissimilarity at initialization to diversity of generated compositions. I can situate that in attention-based diffusion control and kernel sample-repulsion literature, but cannot identify a particular prior work containing that exact surrogate. This distinction concerns an individual proposed mechanism, not merely B’s unusual assembly of familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach is noise-aware multilabel training with calibrated thresholds; for B’s task, it is weakening or annealing classifier-free guidance, or repelling samples during denoising. A’s retreat from explicit hierarchies is a potentially informative negative result, but its replacement remains conventional classifier engineering. B’s batch-level layout shaping exclusively before denoising is a more unexpected central direction. Initial-noise optimization itself is already familiar from InitNO, so the departure is specifically the cross-seed structural objective rather than initialization optimization alone. A provides an implementable pipeline and reports 0.6791 Micro-F1 with component ablations (A page 8). However, optimizing against incompletely annotated validation targets does not by itself establish recovery of genuinely omitted attributes or hierarchical consistency. No clean-label audit or direct hierarchy-consistency test supports that interpretation. The near-total collapse after removing checkpoints or one resolution also lacks sufficient recalibration detail to establish the proposed variance-based explanation. Thus, the demonstrated payoff is narrower than the claimed solution to asymmetric omission noise, and it depends on a costly ensemble (A pages 8–9). B supplies more diagnostic evidence for its narrower practical payoff: repulsion alone increases Vendi from 2.398 to 2.550 against a spherical random-walk control, while geometry ablations show that norm restoration limits quality degradation under aggressive updates (B pages 9–10). These experiments connect interventions to effects rather than relying only on headline benchmark scores. They also reveal that ordinary post-hoc rescaling nearly matches spherical tangent updates, limiting the distinctive value of the elaborate sampler. Important claims need repair: the Jacobian-vector norm is not the asserted Rayleigh quotient (B page 14); fixing the radius preserves energy, not the complete Gaussian distribution; the default fidelity hinge is dormant and its active version fails to protect quality (B page 16); and the roughly 3% overhead claim conflicts with the 63.7% overhead reported in Table 11 (B pages 10 and 15). Fidelity and coverage losses also make the evidence support a diversity–quality tradeoff, not universal Pareto improvement (B pages 6–8). Despite those substantial qualifications, B retains a less routine, explicitly specified intervention with experimental support for controllable diversity gains and an identifiable norm-stabilization mechanism. A’s useful result is primarily conventional score optimization, with its more ambitious noise-and-hierarchy interpretation unestablished. That substantive distinction supports B overall without crediting its breadth or accepting its strongest theoretical and efficiency claims.

A’s building blocks are guidance-direction finite differences, inter-seed spatial Query-Gram repulsion, a fidelity penalty, and spherical Langevin updates (A pages 4–5). Most are recognizable sharpness regularization, attention guidance, or manifold sampling. Its least placeable block is the specific mapping from initial-noise Query-Gram dissimilarity to eventual compositional diversity: I can locate that only broadly in attention-based diffusion control and feature-space repulsion literature, not a particular prior formulation. B’s blocks—an MLP trained with binary cross-entropy, validation-grid threshold selection, and multi-resolution checkpoint averaging—are standard constructions (B pages 5–6). Even its omission-compensating threshold shift is closely connected to established F1-threshold optimization, specifically Lipton and colleagues’ “Thresholding Classifiers to Maximize F1 Score,” and to positive-unlabeled learning. A’s stronger originality therefore rests on a specific representation-to-layout mapping, not simply on assembling four familiar components. For A’s task, the obvious approach is weaker classifier-free guidance or diversity-promoting intervention during denoising; for B’s task, it is a multi-label classifier with omission-aware training and tuned prediction thresholds. A’s central move is instead to separate prospective layouts jointly before denoising, while constraining seed norms. Existing initialization optimization, including InitNO, limits how surprising the initialization stage itself is (A page 3), but the batch-layout objective remains a meaningful departure. B’s rejection of explicit hierarchical geometry could constitute an informative negative result, yet its destination—MLP, threshold tuning, and ensembling—is a familiar practical classification recipe. Its search-branch comparisons do not establish a general failure of geometric approaches (B pages 7–8). Both manuscripts specify actionable mechanisms, but their supported payoffs need narrowing. B establishes a reported score for a conventional prediction pipeline more convincingly than it establishes its claimed mechanism for asymmetric missing-label recovery. A's central idea (A pages 4–5, Eq. 3) is a margin matrix M_yj = τ·V_yj·(1−T_yj) combining a taxonomic-level-overlap prior with multi-layer visual-prototype cosine similarity; its building blocks are placeable in known literature—hierarchy-aware losses (e.g., Wu et al. 2020 deep realistic taxonomic classifier, cited on A page 1; 'making better mistakes'-style hierarchical losses) and class-similarity/difficulty-aware logit margins—so its least placeable block sits only at the subfield level. Its usefulness is weak by its own evidence: the ablation (A pages 7–8) shows removing the logit adjustment costs only +0.0018 error while augmentation drives the result, Table 1 (A page 7) has blank baseline rows, and the paper admits no comparison to standard frequency-based logit adjustment (A page 9), so the claimed payoff of the core mechanism is unsupported. Its departure from the obvious frequency-based approach is modest and ends up effectively self-refuting. Against the obvious lifted-space projection approach, B's move to a reduced space plus barrier polish is a more substantive and central departure than A's mild reweighting. Jointly, B is more useful, at least as new in its least placeable component, and more genuinely surprising.

A's least placeable block is the DLFF step (page 4, eq. 6; Theorem 3 page 10): a norm-bounded log-barrier gradient polish used purely at test time to decouple truncation budget from feasibility while keeping a smooth Jacobian; I can place its ingredients only in the interior-point/barrier genre and in feasibility-restoration heuristics, not in a specific prior HCNN paper, whereas its other blocks (nullspace reparameterization y = yp + Vw, page 3, as in classical null-space methods and DC3-style equality completion; Ruiz-type row equilibration as in OSQP; Douglas–Rachford splitting and matrix-free implicit differentiation as in Πnet/JAXopt) are standard. B's blocks are all placeable: Menon et al. logit adjustment (B page 5, eq. 3–4), taxonomic hierarchy priors (Wu et al. 2020, hierarchical-loss literature), and class prototypes with cosine similarity (prototype-based long-tail work); the product margin τ·V·(1−T) is an assembly rather than a new block. On Useful, A works out its mechanisms and supports the payoff with head-to-head results on identical test instances (Table 1, page 5), five ablations isolating each component (Table 2 and Figures 3–5, pages 6–7), and gradient-accuracy checks (page 4), though Theorem 3's claim that DLFF maps 'any' wK into the interior is shaky since the barrier is undefined for infeasible points, a gap that qualifies rather than overturns the empirical evidence. B's own ablation (Table 2, page 7) shows removing its core logit adjustment costs only +0.0018 error while augmentation drives +0.0242, three baselines in Table 1 (page 7) have no reported numbers, and page 9 concedes no comparison to plain frequency-based logit adjustment, so the central mechanism's payoff is essentially unsupported. On Surprising, the obvious route for A's task is a lifted projection/operator-splitting layer like Πnet; A departs moderately by moving the whole pipeline to reduced space and treating feasibility restoration as a smooth post-hoc flow, which is central to its claims. The obvious route for B's task is frequency-based logit adjustment plus a stronger backbone; B's taxonomy-plus-prototype margin is a predictable refinement, and its most unexpected content—that the proposed adjustment barely matters—is an incidental finding rather than the paper's direction. Both manuscripts assemble largely established mathematical and algorithmic building blocks in novel ways for their respective tasks, but B demonstrates far stronger overall creative quality because its central architectural transformation produces a genuine, well-verified computational and numerical breakthrough, whereas A's central mechanism has a structural symmetry flaw and delivers negligible empirical payoff. Under New, each paper's individual components mostly come from known literature. In A, logit adjustment comes from Menon et al. (2020) (A page 3, 5), taxonomic tree-level overlap is standard in hierarchical classification (A page 4), and multi-layer feature prototypes are standard in metric learning (A page 5); A's least placeable building block is the specific multiplicative pairwise margin formulation M_{y,j} = tau * V_{y,j} * (1 - T_{y,j}) that scales visual prototype similarity by taxonomic dissimilarity (A page 5), which is placeable to the subfield literature of hierarchy- and confusion-aware margin losses in fine-grained recognition. In B, affine nullspace elimination y = y_p + Vw (B page 3), Douglas-Rachford (DR) operator splitting with implicit differentiation (B pages 3-4, following Pi-net and OSQP), and row equilibration are established in numerical optimization and constrained learning; B's least placeable block is the Diffeomorphic Log-Barrier Feasibility Flow (DLFF) step w - grad(phi_B)/(1 + eta * ||grad(phi_B)||_2) used as a smooth post-processing layer for truncated splitting iterates (B page 4, 10), which is placeable to the subfield of barrier and interior-point feasibility restoration. Under Surprising, for A's task of long-tailed fine-grained species classification on iNaturalist 2019, the obvious approach is frequency-based logit adjustment or class re-weighting paired with a taxonomic hierarchy loss. A departs from this by dropping frequency from the margin and instead penalizing visually similar but taxonomically distant classes while applying a softer penalty to close taxonomic neighbors in the same genus (A page 5), and by candidly reporting that its proposed margin contributes almost nothing compared to basic data augmentation (A pages 7-8). For B's task of accelerating and stabilizing hard-constrained neural networks (HCNNs), the obvious approach is to accelerate the lifted-space factorizations or use sophisticated deflated/recycled Krylov solvers for the ill-conditioned implicit backward pass. B makes a much stronger central departure: by projecting the problem into the equality nullspace R^{d - n_eq} and applying a simple unit-norm row scaling to the reduced inequality matrix C_r = C V (B pages 3-4), B reveals that even though the normal matrix condition number kappa(C_r C_r^T) barely changes (4.98e5 to 4.78e5), the lifted DR operator condition number collapses from 12.99 to 2.13 (B page 3, page 6 Table 2b). Consequently, complex deflated-Krylov (DKSR) and residual-correction backward machinery become unnecessary—plain matrix-free BiCGSTAB matches dense LU to 2.4e-10 relative L2 error in 4.9ms (B page 4, pages 6-7 Figure 4)—and models trained with a small iteration budget (K_train = 20) generalize flatly to deep test-time budgets (K_test = 200) (B pages 6-7 Figure 5). Under Useful, the tradeoff between the two papers heavily favors B. In A, although the offline prototype and taxonomic margin pipeline is clearly specified (A pages 4-6), the mechanism is fundamentally mismatched to its stated long-tailed goal: because both V_{y,j} and T_{y,j} are symmetric, the margin M_{y,j} = M_{j,y} is symmetric and completely ignores class frequency, so it cannot asymmetrically shift decision boundaries to protect rare tail species from common head species as claimed (A page 2, page 8 Figure 3). Empirically, A's ablation study (A pages 7-8 Table 2) shows that removing the entire logit adjustment degrades Top-1 error by just 0.0018 (0.2445 vs. 0.2463), which is smaller than removing standard label smoothing (+0.0032) and an order of magnitude smaller than removing standard data augmentation (+0.0242), and A omits any baseline comparison to standard frequency-based logit adjustment (A page 9). B is not without minor flaws requiring repair: its title highlights an 'Amortized' Stiefel hypernetwork that actually fails in Ablation 1 (0% feasibility and 0.38 violation in Table 2a, B page 6, forcing reliance on exact SVD/QR nullspace bases, B pages 3, 8), and the DLFF log-barrier formula phi_B(w) = -sum log(u_tilde_{r,i} - [C_tilde_r w]_i) (Equation 6, B page 4; Theorem 3, B page 10) is strictly defined only on the interior where slacks are positive, leaving unstated how negative (violated) slacks from truncated iterates w_K are clamped or reflected before evaluating the barrier gradient. Nevertheless, B's core reduced-space nullspace embedding and row-equilibrated DR splitting work exceptionally well even without DLFF: across convex and non-convex QP benchmarks (d = 100 to 1000) and SOCPs, B reduces maximum constraint violations to machine precision (1e-13 to 1e-14, up to six orders of magnitude below Pi-net), achieves 100% feasibility and 100% optimality, and trains 2.9x-3.2x faster (B page 5 Table 1, page 6 Table 2, page 10 Table 3).

Every block in A is readily placeable in standard combinatorial optimization works: growing a Steiner tree by iteratively adding the shortest path from the entire current partial tree to an unreached terminal is the classic Takahashi–Matsuyama (1980) Steiner tree heuristic, top-K candidate sampling is the standard Restricted Candidate List mechanism from Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures (GRASP, Feo & Resende, 1995), and applying MCTS over constructive heuristic decisions is standard in the combinatorial routing subfield. While the variance formula itself comes from moment matching for compound Poisson diffusions (e.g., Press, 1967; Ball & Torous, 1985), B's least placeable block—formulating instantaneous total jump-diffusion variance conservation against historical context variance as a multi-horizon neural training regularizer alongside periodic analytical-mean state resets (B page 5)—can only be placed at the broader subfield level of physics-informed/moment-regularized neural SDEs rather than a single prior formulation. Its building blocks are a Merton mixture, loss-optimal point estimation, numerical CDF inversion, stratified inverse-transform sampling, variance matching, and conditional-mean restarting. Most are recognizable statistical or numerical methods. The least placeable assertion is that mean restarting supplies a horizon-independent weak-error guarantee (A pages 5 and 11): I cannot identify a specific prior result supporting that assertion, only the broader SDE-stabilization literature. B consists of UCT-style search, terminal-selection actions, shortest-path attachment to a growing tree, and randomized top-K greedy completion (B pages 4–5). The attachment mechanism closely resembles the Takahashi–Matsuyama shortest-path Steiner heuristic; its least specifically placeable ingredient, treating terminal attachment as a search macro-action, fits macro-action MCTS literature, but I cannot name a particular prior directed-Steiner implementation. Neither paper’s unusual assembly alone establishes new constituent mechanisms. For A’s forecasting task, the obvious approach would be to improve jump-process parameter estimation and generate Monte Carlo forecasts; for B’s routing task, it would be to construct or optimize a cost-aware Steiner tree using shortest-path heuristics or mathematical programming. A redirects attention from model architecture to deterministic, loss-aligned extraction of an already available predictive distribution. B redirects search from individual edges to destination-attachment order, letting Dijkstra construct each path. Both are meaningful but moderate departures: analytical quantiles are natural once the mixture is explicit, and B’s path-level construction remains close to established Steiner heuristics. B’s advertised neural-symbolic departure is not operationally demonstrated—the described solver is MCTS plus graph algorithms, without a specified LLM role. The distinction is in how much useful payoff survives scrutiny. A works out its inference transformations and regularization explicitly (A pages 4–5), and its fixed-checkpoint and component-removal experiments provide interpretable attribution: analytical inversion improves p-MAE from 14.9 to 14.2, while stratification reduces oracle minMAE from 4.86 to 2.79 (A page 7). These support practical improvements over the stated sampling pipeline, not proof of better-calibrated trajectory distributions. Indeed, reusing each quantile across time in equation 7 changes the joint increment dependence, and resetting trajectories to their mean destroys variance, invalidating the claimed general weak-error argument. The regularizer also worsens the 14-step results despite improving the 28-step results (A page 12). Thus A needs substantial qualification, particularly around ‘exact’ trajectory inference and universal stability, but its narrower inference benefit has direct experimental support. B’s core algorithm is implementable and sensibly exploits already-paid tree edges through multi-source shortest paths (B page 5). Exact attachment costs, however, do not imply optimal Steiner subtrees or global optimality. More importantly, its central empirical payoff is unresolved in the supplied text: B page 6 reports 627.10, whereas Table 1 on B page 7 lists 1090.78 for the proposed method against the same baselines. The caption on B page 8 introduces yet another, incompatible lowest-cost claim. Its ablations conflate rollout changes with state-abstraction changes, and the rejection of cheaper variants for instability lacks corresponding success-rate measurements (B pages 6 and 8). B also acknowledges that throughput constraints and dynamic-network evaluation are absent (B page 9). Consequently, A’s modest but more directly isolated practical correction outweighs B’s attractive search abstraction, whose claimed competitive and robust payoff cannot presently be reconciled with its reported evidence.

Regarding the obvious approach for each task and how far each manuscript departs from it (Surprising): for A's task of low-latency, topology-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) expert placement and replication, a competent approach would typically implement greedy Longest Processing Time (LPT) bin-packing and sequential replica allocation in a compiled C++/CUDA kernel or run an approximate solver asynchronously; A departs from this by reformulating placement entirely as loop-free PyTorch tensor operations, replacing stateful bin-packing with a static boustrophedon (snake) scatter (A pages 4-5) and casting sequential greedy replica assignment as a parallel D'Hondt quotient matrix with global top-k selection (A page 5). For B's task of attributing multi-token generated spans across long contexts and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning chains, the obvious approach would be to compute layer-local continuous vector similarities (or whitened norms) and recursively propagate attribution by weighting intermediate reasoning tokens by their first-hop relevance scores; B departs much more counterintuitively by collapsing the aggregated final-layer target representation into a single binary sign vector s_S in {-1, +1}^D, projecting intermediate-layer head value-output vectors across all depths onto this fixed final-layer sign vector (B pages 3-5), and using an unweighted target (w_j = 1) over intermediate reasoning tokens during recursive attribution because weighting by first-hop relevance scores actively distorts the orientation signal (B pages 5-6, 10). Regarding prior art for each paper's building blocks (New): A's components can be placed in specific known formulations—two-level node/GPU packing is standard in distributed MoE serving (A pages 3-4), boustrophedon assignment is a classic zig-zag scheduling heuristic (A page 4), and the D'Hondt quotient matrix is the textbook proportional apportionment algorithm directly vectorized via tensor broadcasting (A page 5). In contrast, while B builds on residual-stream L1 proximity (Ferrando et al., 2022) and multi-token recursive attribution (Pan et al., 2025) (B page 3), its least placeable building block—linearizing L1 proximity into a single final-layer binary sign vector applied across all intermediate Transformer layers alongside an unweighted sign-orientation CoT recursion (B pages 3-6)—cannot be placed in a specific prior work and is only placeable within the broader subfield literature of Transformer mechanistic and residual-stream interpretability. Finally, comparing whether the mechanisms work and deliver their claimed payoffs (Useful): A defines its snake scatter and D'Hondt quotient equations (A pages 4-5), but its empirical payoff fails to support its claims and exhibits internal inconsistencies. A offers the stronger overall contribution, narrowly: its intervention is modest but mechanically coherent, whereas B’s more adventurous proposal has a load-bearing mismatch between its mathematical construction and its claimed mechanism. For New, A decomposes into BEV fusion, coordinate embeddings, map distance fields and sigmoid gating (A pages 5–6). Its hardest-to-place ingredient is treating distance-to-map-support as a positional signal; I can locate that only in map-aware geometric perception, although the broader use of maps to improve detection already appears in HDNET: Exploiting HD Maps for 3D Object Detection. B decomposes into masked frame reconstruction, log-rotation and commutator targets, heat transport and integrated decoding (B pages 3–4). Its hardest-to-place claim is that the proposed log-commutator residual supplies a useful protein-packing target; I cannot name a specific earlier protein-learning treatment. The underlying moving-frame/DEC machinery and heat transport are recognizable from established differential geometry and The Vector Heat Method. Neither manuscript earns additional newness simply from assembling established ingredients. The obvious direction for A’s task would be to improve LiDAR–camera BEV fusion and incorporate available maps through feature fusion. Moving map information into a gated positional encoding is a relatively small departure. For B, the obvious direction would be masked reconstruction of backbone coordinates or local frames with geometric attention. Replacing those targets with connection/curvature supervision and an integrating decoder is a substantially more unexpected central move, independently of whether its mathematics works. B also reports meaningful practical evidence: its matched comparison improves external accuracy from 51.10 to 61.79, with further gains from attention biases (B page 5). However, its stated connection is pure gauge: multiplying E_i^T E_j around any closed loop telescopes exactly to the identity. Consequently, the holonomy defect defined on B page 4 cannot identify hinges or transport frustration; B page 9 explicitly acknowledges that true holonomy vanishes. The nonzero truncated log-commutator residual is therefore not genuine curvature of that connection, and the holonomy-dependent masking results on B page 11 require some different, unspecified statistic. Moreover, exponentiating a sum of noncommuting rotations is not generally the claimed path integration (B page 4). The reported gains could support a heuristic auxiliary-feature objective, but they do not establish the advertised transport-aware mechanism. A’s coordinate and map embeddings, convex gate and additive BEV injection are directly implementable. Its ablations provide limited evidence for the intervention: removing semantic encoding reduces the reported score from 0.1763 to 0.1746, while removing gating reduces it to 0.1706 (A page 9). A nevertheless needs substantial qualification: its TP/(TP+FP+FN) expression is not mAP (A page 7), and it supplies neither isolated yaw/dimension improvements nor map-corruption tests (A pages 9–10). Thus its claimed geometric payoff is not established. The distinction is that narrowing A’s claims leaves an intelligible, testable map-conditioning mechanism, whereas B’s central geometric explanation requires reconstruction. B’s greater surprise and stronger reported transfer comparisons do not quite overcome that foundational problem.

B combines LSTM regression with a weighted adjacent-hidden-state penalty (B page 2). Even that putatively distinctive block is specifically placeable as temporal activation regularization in Merity et al.’s Regularizing and Optimizing LSTM Language Models. Calling it compositional regularization does not introduce a new compositional operation. For A’s task, the obvious approach is to contrastively align an efficient spiking point encoder with pretrained image/text representations while controlling inference costs; for B’s task, it is to exploit expression syntax or enforce consistency between representations of subexpressions and their compositions. Against these baselines, A’s rejection of elaborate geometric and timing modules is a modest, task-consistent reversal rather than a radically unexpected direction (A page 8). B takes a stranger central detour by substituting temporal smoothness for structural composition and then reporting failure (B pages 2–4). That directional departure deserves recognition independently of whether its mechanism works. The decisive distinction is the supported payoff. A specifies distribution-matching losses and fixed-degree graph propagation sufficiently to explain how training alignment and inexpensive spatial aggregation could improve recognition (A pages 5–6). Its reported full-model improvements from 82.1% to 83.75% on ModelNet40 and 40.1% to 41.47% on Objaverse-LVIS, together with component ablations, support a bounded practical contribution (A pages 7–8). Important qualifications remain: the Student-t kernel does not guarantee the claimed scale invariance or nonvanishing gradients; MMD alone slightly reduces LVIS accuracy in Table 2; energy savings are modeled rather than demonstrated on deployed hardware (A pages 9–10); and the isolated rejected-module experiments operate near chance, limiting their generality (A page 14). Nevertheless, there is evidence for the functioning intervention beyond its explanatory claims. B’s penalty is implementable, but minimizing successive-state differences enforces smoothness, not operator-sensitive composition: constant hidden states minimize it without representing arithmetic structure. Consequently, reduced penalty values cannot establish that compositional representations were learned, as claimed on B pages 3–4. The reported lack of improvement usefully cautions against this particular smoothness regularizer, but cannot establish the inadequacy of genuine compositional regularization. The unspecified prediction tolerance and insufficiently defined compositional train/test split further restrict that conclusion (B page 3). Overall, A’s incremental and partly overstated proposal offers a more substantive, experimentally supported intervention, whereas B’s more unusual direction rests on a misidentified mechanism. That tradeoff favors A’s overall creative quality.

A proposes a hidden-state smoothness penalty as a 'compositional regularizer' for an LSTM on arithmetic (A page 2, Eq. 1) and reports that it fails to improve generalization while increasing operator complexity hurts regardless (A pages 3–4, appendices pages 5–8). Its least placeable block—temporal smoothness of successive hidden states—is placeable in the slow-feature/temporal-coherence regularization genre, so New is modest, and the mapping from smoothness to 'compositionality' is weakly argued. But the manuscript is internally consistent: the mechanism is specified, the ablations (λ sweep, embedding dim, attention, RNN vs LSTM, dropout) coherently support the stated negative conclusion, and the central move—showing the expected regularization approach fails and openly reporting it—is a genuine departure from the obvious positive-result direction. B assembles PageRank-style centrality on a pairwise-cost conflict graph (B page 4, Eqs. 1–3), multi-start greedy with depth-2 lookahead (B page 5), and bounded VND (B pages 5–6); each block is placeable (PageRank, lookahead greedy, Hansen & Mladenovic VNS), with the asymmetric pairwise-delay transition matrix being the least placeable but still a subfield-level heuristic. B's Surprising value lies in the assembly and the swap from learned to pure algorithmic search, but its Useful case collapses under inspection: the abstract claims 3610.1 vs SMF 85.2 and ADRS 92.4 (B page 1) yet concedes AdaEvolve scores 4317.0 (B page 6), Table 1 lists 'Ours' as 3717.47 while the text attributes 3717.4 to a rejected 'Retrograde' variant (B pages 6–7), the ablation table mixes 'Failed Audit' alternatives rather than genuine component removals (B page 7), Figure 3 compares against FCFS/EDF/GA that appear nowhere in Table 1, and a cited 'evolutionary agents' reference is an orthopaedic trauma paper (B page 9). These inconsistencies make B's payoff unverifiable and its load-bearing SOTA claims self-contradicted. Weighing the tradeoffs jointly, A's limited but coherent, honestly reported negative result with a surprising central framing outranks B's superficially richer but internally inconsistent and largely recombinatory pipeline.

For Useful, Manuscript A's central proposal is a three-stage algorithmic scheduler that prioritizes transactions via conflict-graph PageRank, builds candidate schedules with a 35-start depth-2 lookahead greedy heuristic, and refines the best schedule via bounded first-improvement VND (A pages 2, 4-6). The mechanism is mathematically and algorithmically worked out in detail with explicit equations and neighborhood bounds (A pages 4-6), and its internal ablation study supports the claimed payoff: adding VND improves the raw scheduling score from 3496.5 to 3610.1, and trading depth-3 lookahead for depth-2 lookahead to expand multi-start candidates from 15 to 35 reduces makespan to 276.0 (A page 7, Table 2). However, A suffers from factual and reporting flaws that put parts of its empirical comparison in need of repair: it compares its raw score (3610.1) directly against normalized baseline scores for SMF (85.2) and ADRS (92.4) while listing AdaEvolve as 89.2 on A page 4 but 4317.0 in Table 1 (A pages 1, 4, 6, 7); Table 1 lists a rejected backward-chaining variant's score (3717.47) as the proposed method's score (A page 7); it contradicts itself on whether it beats AdaEvolve (A pages 6, 8); and it includes a false citation attribution ([Musick et al., 2026], an orthopedic trauma study on sacral fractures, cited for evolutionary agents on A pages 4, 9). Even with those reporting defects, A's core algorithmic mechanism is coherent, actionable, and demonstrably effective in its ablation. By contrast, Manuscript B's central proposal—penalizing ||h_{t+1} - h_t||^2 to induce additive compositional representations in an LSTM (B page 2)—fails both mechanistically and empirically. Penalizing hidden-state changes forces temporal constancy across steps rather than compositional state updates when reading new operators and operands, and B's own experiments show the regularizer fails to improve test accuracy and often degrades learning (B pages 1, 3-4, 6). Moreover, B's experimental setup is in need of repair even as a negative report: it omits dataset vocabulary, expression length, and the tolerance threshold defining accuracy (B page 3), and outside of stating an approximate 84% baseline accuracy (B page 3), it provides no quantitative tables or numerical values in the text for any regularized model or ablation across B pages 3-8. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of static conflict-aware transaction scheduling is to greedily append transactions by local conflict degree or minimal incremental makespan, optionally followed by a standard single-neighborhood local search (A pages 1, 3); the obvious approach to B's task of neural compositional generalization on arithmetic is to introduce tree/hierarchical architectural inductive biases or semantic consistency regularization across equivalent expressions (B pages 1-2). While B departs from standard positive reporting by presenting a negative result (B pages 1, 4), its technical move of applying a temporal smoothing penalty to an LSTM is routine, and the failure of state-freezing regularization on multi-operator arithmetic is entirely predictable. Conversely, A makes a substantive central departure in how it assembles its pipeline: mapping asymmetric pairwise execution delays into a Markov transition matrix to compute global PageRank priorities, using those priorities to prune a multi-start depth-2 lookahead constructor, and coupling it with a bounded three-operator VND loop (A pages 4-6). Despite A's baseline reporting and citation errors under Useful, its fully worked-out algorithmic mechanism, harder-to-place conflict-matrix block, and non-trivial multi-stage assembly give A stronger overall creative quality than B.

For New, we break each manuscript into its constituent building blocks and examine the least placeable component. Manuscript A's central technical block is the regularization term $L_{\text{comp}} = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \|h_{t+1} - h_t\|^2$ added to an LSTM's mean squared error objective (A page 2, Equations 1 and 2), supplemented by standard sequence-modeling ablations on embedding size, attention, RNN cells, and dropout (A pages 5-8). Even though A labels this penalty 'compositional regularization,' the mathematical mechanism itself is specifically placeable in the existing recurrent network regularization literature—most notably Temporal Activation Regularization (TAR, Merity et al., 2017) and standard temporal smoothness penalties in state-space sequence models. In contrast, Manuscript B combines a taxonomic lineage similarity matrix $T_{i,j}$ over six biological ranks (B page 4, Equation 1), offline multi-layer feature prototype cosine similarities $V_{i,j}$ (B page 5, Equation 2), and a pairwise logit margin $M_{y,j} = \tau \cdot V_{y,j} \cdot (1 - T_{y,j})$ subtracted from non-target logits during training (B page 5, Equations 3 and 4). While hierarchical taxonomic distances and prototype similarities appear individually in fine-grained and long-tailed recognition literature (such as Menon et al., 2020 and Wu et al., 2020), the specific multiplicative formulation $V_{y,j}(1 - T_{y,j})$ that dampens visual similarity penalties between close taxonomic relatives while penalizing visually similar but taxonomically distant confusions can only be placed broadly within the subfield of hierarchical cost-sensitive and margin-based classification rather than in a single pre-existing work. For Useful, Manuscript A's mechanism is both conceptually flawed and empirically unsupported. Penalizing $\|h_{t+1} - h_t\|^2$ forces hidden states to remain nearly static across time steps rather than composing operators and operands hierarchically; consequently, as A reports, the regularizer fails to improve test accuracy on synthetic arithmetic expressions and degrades learning as $\lambda$ increases (A pages 1, 3, and 4). Furthermore, A lacks critical experimental evidence: it never specifies the operand ranges, expression lengths, or accuracy tolerance threshold for its 1,000-sample synthetic dataset (A pages 2-3), and its extracted text contains only qualitative figure captions with no numerical tables beyond a single mention of 'approximately 84%' baseline accuracy (A page 3). Manuscript B, by contrast, presents a fully worked-out offline-prior and online-training algorithm (B pages 4-6, Algorithm 1) evaluated on the large-scale iNaturalist 2019 benchmark (268,243 images across 1,010 species) under strict ImageNet-1K pre-training controls (B pages 4 and 6). B provides concrete quantitative evidence in Tables 1 and 2 (B page 7), showing that its full method achieves 0.2445 Top-1 Error, outperforming both seven alternative dynamic-margin search variants (0.2549 to 0.3341 in Table 1) and component ablations including single-layer prototypes (0.2461) and no logit adjustment (0.2463 in Table 2). The main tradeoff in B's usefulness—which B candidly analyzes (B pages 7-9)—is that the net error reduction over no logit adjustment is modest (+0.0018) compared to standard data augmentation (+0.0242), the hyperparameter $\tau$ value is omitted from the implementation text (B page 6), and a direct tabular comparison against static frequency-based logit adjustment is missing (B page 9). Even with that tradeoff, B's mechanism works and delivers a verified positive payoff on a realistic task, whereas A's mechanism fails to work. For Surprising, the obvious approach to A's task of arithmetic compositional generalization would be to introduce syntactic tree/modular architectures or invariance regularizers across substituted sub-expressions, whereas A instead applies a simple temporal smoothness penalty to an LSTM and frames the paper around its negative result (A pages 1-4). For B's task of long-tailed fine-grained classification, the obvious approach is to scale logit margins by static class frequencies to boost rare classes or to increase margins between closely related species within the same taxon. B departs from this expected direction in two central ways: it replaces class-frequency margins entirely with pairwise visual-taxonomic interaction margins, and it counterintuitively uses $(1 - T_{y,j})$ to soften penalties between taxonomically close neighbors while targeting convergent visual confusion across distant taxa (B page 5, Equation 3). Moreover, comparing B's Table 1 and Table 2 (B page 7) reveals a non-obvious empirical insight: naive dynamic confusion margins and visual-only prototype margins (0.2549 to 0.3341) actually degrade the unadjusted baseline (0.2463), and only damping the multi-layer visual prototypes by taxonomic distance $(1 - T_{y,j})$ stabilizes the margin enough to surpass the baseline (0.2445).
