A's task is to measure how label noise affects calibration, and its approach is exactly the obvious one: inject symmetric/asymmetric noise, train ResNet-18, report ECE and temperature scaling (A pages 2-3). Every building block—synthetic flip noise, ECE/reliability diagrams, temperature scaling—is standard material from the label-noise and calibration literatures (Guo et al.-style calibration, Ghosh/Song surveys A cites), and the finding that noisy labels yield overconfident, miscalibrated networks is already a known consequence of memorization. Its evidence is also internally inconsistent: the text says Figure 3 compares temperature scaling and label smoothing while the caption compares ResNet-18 to a basic CNN (A page 4), robust loss functions are discussed as tested but never appear in the methodology (A pages 3-5), reliability diagrams are 'not shown' (A page 6), and SVHN results are asserted without data (A page 7). B's task is dynamic expert replication/placement for MoE inference, where the obvious directions are greedy LPT bin-packing or an LP solver; B departs by recasting hierarchical node-then-load sorting as a single scalar composite key (node_ID minus normalized load, Eq. 2, B page 5) and replacing sequential packing with a vectorized zigzag scatter (Eq. 3, B page 5). Those blocks are individually placeable—combined-key lexsort is a common numpy/PyTorch idiom and snake-order assignment is a classic scheduling heuristic—so New is modest, but the assembly is a less predictable central move than A's. B's usefulness is compromised: the headline comparison places a raw 0.1461 against leaderboard scores on an incompatible converted scale (B page 7), and the abstract's claim of avoiding slow penalties is contradicted by the 4.91 ms time exceeding the 2 ms budget and a speed score of 0.0068 (B pages 6-7). Still, B's mechanism is fully specified and supported by a same-scale ablation against water-filling, Latin-square templates, and inverse-locality variants (B page 8), plus a candid limitations section (B page 9), whereas A's central observation rests on figures whose descriptions do not match and on untested claims. Weighing a predictable study with muddled evidence against a flawed but mechanistically concrete and more directionally unexpected heuristic, B has stronger overall creative quality.

Evaluated relative to their respective fields and research tasks, Manuscript B demonstrates substantially stronger overall creative quality than Manuscript A when considering New, Useful, and Surprising jointly. Regarding New, both manuscripts assemble familiar building blocks from their subfields rather than introducing wholly unprecedented mathematical primitives. Manuscript A relies on standard Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (Ho et al., 2020) on 2D toy distributions (A pages 3, 5) combined with a k-nearest neighbor set-overlap metric, LSPS (A page 4, Eq. 1-2), which is a standard neighborhood-preservation formulation from the dimensionality-reduction and manifold-learning literature (such as trustworthiness/continuity and rank-based k-NN overlap criteria), added as a scalar penalty to the training loss (A page 4, Eq. 3). Manuscript B relies on a pre-trained CodeBERT dual-encoder with L2-normalized cosine similarity and cross-entropy loss (Feng et al., 2020; standard contrastive retrieval literature) coupled with linear assignment / expected position ranking (Cao et al., 2007) (B pages 5-6). Its least placeable building block is constructing synthetic bidirectional code-boundary scaffolds by concatenating adjacent code cells (c_j, c_{j+1}) to represent the |C|+1 inter-cell gaps in a notebook (B pages 4-5), a domain-specific representation placeable in the subfield literature on computational notebook structure recovery and Kaggle AI4Code competition solutions. Where the two manuscripts diverge sharply is in Surprising and Useful. For Surprising, the obvious approach to Manuscript A's task—preserving local structure in low-dimensional diffusion models—is to add a neighborhood- or distance-preservation regularization term directly to the diffusion training objective, which is the exact route A takes without further conceptual departure (A page 4). Conversely, for Manuscript B's task—reconstructing the global order of shuffled markdown cells in computational notebooks—the obvious approach is either flat full-notebook sequence modeling or localized pairwise precedence classification (predicting whether cell A precedes cell B) (B pages 1-2). Manuscript B departs centrally from both by exploiting the invariant order of executable code cells to reframe global ordering as matching shuffled markdown cells against the |C|+1 synthetic bidirectional code boundaries (B pages 4-6). This reframing also yields unexpected empirical insights in B's ablations: adding a margin ranking loss slightly degrades performance (-0.0007 Kendall tau) compared to plain cross-entropy over boundary slots, and replacing the code-specific CodeBERT backbone with a generic RoBERTa model slightly improves performance (+0.0009), showing that the structural bipartite slot formulation and bidirectional context carry the task rather than domain-specific pre-training or complex ranking losses (B pages 8-9, Table 2). For Useful, Manuscript A's central proposal is in need of fundamental repair and fails to deliver its claimed payoff. Specifically, A defines LSPS via the discrete set intersection of k-nearest neighbors |N_k(x_i) ∩ N_k(\hat{x}_i)| (A page 4, Eq. 1-2) and adds L_{LSPS} = 1 - LSPS directly to the gradient-descent training objective (A pages 4-5, Eq. 3). Because discrete k-NN set intersection is piecewise constant with zero gradient almost everywhere and A specifies no differentiable relaxation, the loss cannot provide meaningful gradient signal. Empirically, A's own text admits that LSPS on the circle dataset changed "from 0.100098 to 0.100098" and on the moons dataset "from 0.10066 to 0.10066" (A page 8)—literally zero change—while Table 1 omits all baseline LSPS values (listed as "—" on A page 6) and the manuscript leaves broken placeholders and truncated sentences (e.g., "Figure 1: PLEASE FILL IN CAPTION HERE" and "Tables 1 and ??" on A page 6; "only about 10" on A page 9). In contrast, Manuscript B's mechanism works and delivers a strongly supported payoff on the 160,000-notebook AI4Code benchmark, achieving a 0.8356 Kendall tau score (and 0.8375 with argmax inference), outperforming 15 competing architectural baselines in Table 1 (B pages 7-8). Manuscript B does contain a minor technical inconsistency in Section 3.5 (B page 6): Algorithm 1 specifies one-to-one LinearSumAssignment on the negated similarity matrix, whereas the text notes that multiple markdown cells can map to a single boundary gap and that the primary solver actually computes a continuous position expectation E[pos_i] = \sum_j P(b_j|m_i) \cdot j or row-wise argmax (B page 6; Figure 3 on B page 5). Even accounting for this minor terminology gap between strict one-to-one assignment and many-to-one slot expectation, B's boundary-matching mechanism coherently eliminates cyclic pairwise inconsistencies, avoids full-notebook token truncation, and proves through controlled ablations that bidirectional boundary scaffolding is a load-bearing mechanism whose removal drops Kendall tau by 0.0437 (B pages 8-9, Table 2).

These are also familiar components. Its least readily placeable claim is the mapping from instability on MedMNIST to difficulties adapting to agricultural pests: I can locate that only broadly in negative-transfer/domain-shift literature, not in a specific established result. That limited specificity does not establish a new method, and the unusual dataset assembly should count as direction rather than component novelty. For A’s task, the obvious approach is a controlled comparison of dense, sparse, and local attention using predictive quality and computational cost; A follows that direction directly. For B’s failure-diagnosis task, the obvious approach is testing a pest classifier across environmental corruptions or farm-to-farm shifts. Its substantial excursion into satellite, medical, and generic-object datasets is a more unexpected central move (B pages 2–4). The negative-results framing alone is not surprising given its stated task, and the unexpected dataset choice is not automatically useful. The decisive distinction is that B develops at least a concrete, testable diagnostic mechanism. Specified brightness, contrast, blur, and affine perturbations, together with ERS, operationalize relative accuracy retention under those particular changes (B pages 5–6). Its learning-rate experiment also reports qualitative outcomes, although the extracted text supplies no numerical results sufficient to establish effect sizes or reliability. A leaves its sparse selection rule unspecified, supplies no attention-specific computational measurements, and has an empty Results section before declaring sparse attention superior in accuracy, perplexity, and overhead (A pages 2–3). Its central recommendation therefore lacks demonstrated support. B nevertheless needs substantial repair: separate training behavior on unrelated datasets does not demonstrate transfer to pest detection, no joint-training or adaptation mechanism is explained, and synthetic corruptions do not establish real-world agricultural robustness (B pages 2–4). ERS also measures relative retention, not adequate absolute performance. These limitations sharply narrow B’s payoff to an actionable stress-testing protocol and qualitative observations. I choose B because that narrower mechanism is more worked out and its investigation takes a less predictable direction, despite modest component novelty and unsupported broader conclusions—not because its claimed domain-adaptation explanation succeeds.

A studies how symmetric/asymmetric label noise degrades calibration (ECE) of ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/MNIST/Fashion-MNIST and tests temperature scaling/label smoothing as mitigations. Its building blocks are all placeable: label-noise taxonomies (Song et al. survey, Ghosh et al. robust losses), ECE/reliability diagrams and temperature scaling (Guo et al. 2017 genre), and the noise-calibration interplay (Zhao et al. 2020, Adebayo et al. 2023, both cited by A). The obvious approach to 'does label noise hurt calibration' is exactly what A does, so Surprising is low, though the 'asymmetric noise worse for ECE than accuracy' observation (A page 3) is a mild empirical twist. Usefully, A reports concrete numbers (accuracy ~85%→60%, ECE up to 0.35, page 3; hyperparameters page 6) and a coherent, if modest and partly inconsistent, pipeline (page 4 describes a Figure 3 about CNN vs ResNet while the text promises temperature scaling vs label smoothing; reliability diagrams 'not shown' page 6). B proposes a 'framework' for preference-based evaluation metrics to improve diffusion controllability, drawing on preference learning and recommender-system evaluation (Clarke et al., Sun et al., page 3) and RLHF-for-diffusion (Black et al., Clark et al., page 2). Its one potentially less placeable block—recommender-style preference metrics as a controllability signal for diffusion—is never actually defined: no metric formula, no preference format, no mechanism for how constraints C enter generation (pages 2–3). The only results table (page 3) reports baseline training time, eval loss, and KL divergence on toy 2D datasets, with no preference-metric numbers, no ablation data despite claiming ablations, and the text asserts 'significant improvement' without evidence. So B's direction is somewhat less expected than A's, but it is asserted rather than worked out and its payoff is unsupported, whereas A, though conventional, delivers a mechanism and measurable results that follow from its design. A's grounded, actionable empirical finding outweighs B's unspecified and unvalidated framework.

(2020) and common 2D toy diffusion implementations. For B's task of enhancing diffusion model controllability for user preferences, the obvious approach is to formulate a reward model, classifier guidance term, or direct preference optimization objective and evaluate alignment on preference-annotated data. In contrast, B's central proposal is in need of fundamental repair: Section 4 (B pages 2–3) repeats abstract claims that preferences are structured as constraints C and evaluated with new metrics without providing a single mathematical definition, algorithm, constraint format, or metric formula.
